documents.title: Durable SQL queues and workers
documents.text:
# Durable SQL queues and workers

The `app,database` features provide explicit SQLite/PostgreSQL project queues
and independent worker processes. Submission persists immutable task input and
host contracts before execution. Workers reuse the existing durable run,
workflow, PEER and session controllers; a second job log never decides that an
unknown external write is safe to repeat.

Default features remain empty. File-based/local execution and `AgentTask` remain
compatible, with Rust 1.86. Queues are explicitly configured by a trusted local
administrator. The multi-user JSON service uses the same SQL project and live
role/token checks. The existing browser UI is the local operator UI; queue
submission/control currently uses the queue API or CLI. Legacy `job.active`
fields describe process-local workers. **Use queue job state and its runtime
bindings for distributed activity**, including a worker running on another host.

## Setup and migration

1. Stop old API hosts and workers. Back up the complete database and separately
   protect host configs, credentials, model weights and external tool data.
2. Build/install with `app,database` and run `taskloom database-migrate` against
   the intended database. This explicitly upgrades schema v1/v2 to **v3** in
   one transaction. No live database-clock lease may remain. PostgreSQL locks
   the lease table during the barrier. Unknown versions/downgrades are refused.
3. Configure model/prices, tools, role grants and SQL tenant/project normally.
   Initialize a reviewed generation quota separately; queue capacity does not
   replace the generation spending ledger.
4. Configure queue capacity, then start the project API and separate workers
   with the same frozen host contracts and SQL dataset/project identity.

Schema v3 adds `taskloom_jobs` and `taskloom_job_bindings` with claim/resource
indexes. Existing dataset UUID, runtime envelopes, budgets, quotes, approvals
and exact host bindings are preserved. V1/v2 binaries fail schema/ownership
checks after migration; do not mix them into a running v3 deployment. There is
no automatic file-to-SQL import, partial journal import or schema downgrade.
Restore a complete backup with its matching binary when a rollback is required.

The retained v2 migration probe rebuilds the actual pre-queue SDK at `8f681b0`
in an ignored, separate source directory. Copy
`examples/database/legacy_owner.rs` to that archive's
`examples/old_queue_owner.rs` and build it plus `database_native` with
`--all-features --target-dir target/archived-v2-build`. Always use a different
Cargo target directory from the current checkout: equal package names/versions
can otherwise collide in cached artifacts. The lease-only fixture refuses any SDK schema other than v2.
Pass those binaries as `--old-owner` and `--old-probe` to
`accept_quota_migration.py --source-version 2`, using copies of the retained
v2 native SQLite file/dump and matching `--native-campaign`. The probe verifies
a real old process blocks upgrade while live, kills only that owned process,
waits its original lease, then verifies record/quota preservation and old-binary
schema rejection. It makes no model/tool call and is not a rolling-upgrade or
old-binary native-dispatch benchmark. Original databases stay untouched.

```powershell
cargo build --all-features --bin taskloom --example multiuser_host
taskloom --config project.json database-migrate
# limits.json: {"max_open_jobs":24,"max_running":4}
taskloom --config project.json queue-configure limits.json 0 local-admin "reviewed project capacity"
# task.json: {"type":"run","id":"hello","prompt":"Summarize the supplied task."}
taskloom --config project.json queue-submit task.json local-operator
taskloom --config project.json worker worker-a
# Another independent process, same host contract and namespace:
taskloom --config project.json worker worker-b
```

`queue-configure` needs expected **policy** revision, operator and note. A JSON
`null` disables new queue admission/claiming. It never erases jobs, refunds
generation uncertainty or reopens the multi-user service's direct execution
routes. Already executing owners can finish. Explicit control is required to
stop them. Host-contract changes require all open jobs to be resolved first;
use the original config/grants for recovery rather than rewriting input.

`max_open_jobs` (1–100000) includes pending, running, waiting, paused and failed
jobs. `max_running` (1–256, within open capacity) bounds live queue/runtime
owners across processes. Reducing it constrains recovery as well as new work;
unexpired original owners are not retroactively killed. Expired jobs without
live runtime owners can be recovered without consuming stale capacity forever.

Workers are trusted host programs with their configured model/tool credentials;
ordinary service users do not receive these credentials. Custom model adapters
and SDK workers must use the guarded SQL stores and priced generation
reservations. The built-in Application worker does so. CLI queue inspection,
resume requests and control requests do not initialize model/MCP clients.
Submission/configuration/worker boot currently validates the configured host
model and MCP bindings and therefore needs their named credentials, even though
enqueue/configuration performs no model generation or tool invocation.

The source service example listens on loopback. Use a host-configured TLS reverse
proxy when serving remote clients; keep database/model/tool credentials in the
backend environment. Supervise the API and worker processes independently,
monitor Failed/Waiting jobs and unresolved effects, and drain admission/workers
before backup or host-contract changes. SQLite is one durable database file/WAL
on a suitable local filesystem; PostgreSQL supports separate process hosts using
the same project database. The supplied acceptance uses one local host and a
real loopback PostgreSQL container, not a multi-machine failover or production
network partition campaign.

## Task input and service roles

The API accepts only the following task forms; input cannot install tools,
select another database or grant itself permissions:

```json
{"type":"run","id":"answer","prompt":"A bounded user request"}
```

```json
{"type":"session_turn","id":"conversation","turn":"first","prompt":"A bounded request"}
```

Create the conversation explicitly first. Different open jobs cannot occupy the
same conversation, including approval/recovery waits. A completed turn permits
the next queued turn; failed terminal turns still require the existing explicit
abandon operation. Historical child runs retain their original queue association.

For a workflow, call `/workflow-design/preview`, review its registered roles,
limits and exact input, then submit:

```json
{"type":"workflow","launch":{"request":{"id":"flow","input":{},"definition":{"nodes":[]},"peer":null,"limits":{}},"preview_key":"the actual reviewed preview_key"}}
```

This schematic example omits a useful graph and complete limits; use the real
validated request returned by your preview. DAG and PEER tasks use the same role
compiler and frozen task definitions as local execution. The worker rejects a
changed preview/host configuration before dispatch. Reusing a job identity with
different exact input or resource is refused. Repeating the same submission
returns its original receipt and submitter, including after completion.

The single-operator routes below are under `/api`. In the authenticated service
they are under `/tenants/T/projects/P/api`, with per-request role checks:

| Route | Permission and meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /queue` | Reader: policy and this host's binding |
| `GET /queue/jobs` | Reader: bounded job listing (1000 records/64MiB) |
| `GET /queue/jobs/ID` | Reader: job plus current runtime/child associations |
| `POST /queue/jobs` | Runner: `{task, actor}`; service replaces actor with authenticated user |
| `POST /queue/jobs/ID/resume` | Runner: exact `expected_revision`, actor and note |
| `POST /queue/jobs/ID/control` | Operator: exact revision, `action: pause|cancel|abandon`, actor and note |

Approvers retain their existing exact-ticket approval/rejection routes, and
operators retain explicit child reconciliation and failed-turn abandonment.
Neither operation dispatches work. An explicit queue resume is required after
approval/reconciliation. Actor spoofing is rejected by replacing body identity
at the authenticated boundary. Role changes, expiry and revocation are checked
on every request. Revocation does not undo an already accepted task: explicitly
cancel it when required.

Once the project has a queue policy, the multi-user service refuses its direct
run/workflow/session dispatch/resume/pause/cancel routes with 409. Users must use
queue admission/control, including while queue admission is disabled. This
prevents bypassing queue capacity through the old endpoints. Trusted local SDK
and single-operator administration remain separate host authority. A previously
queue-bound runtime cannot dispatch without its current queue capability even
through a plain `db.runs(scope)` handle.

## Ownership, interruption and recovery

Claiming a job, increasing its attempt count and marking it Running is one SQL
transaction. Database time determines renewable lease validity. A candidate is
eligible only when both its queue owner and every associated runtime owner have
expired. A live owner is never stolen. Recovery claims are prioritized over new
pending jobs; healthy workers then take jobs in creation/ID order. This is not a
guarantee of fair CPU allocation among worker processes.

Run/workflow/session stores bind to the exact queue capability. Runtime writes
and pre-dispatch checks verify both fences, with another check before commit
after potentially expensive decoding/accounting. Generation reservations still
commit before each provider attempt. Removing a capability cannot authorize
dispatch through a plain SQL handle. Lease loss or an unverified monitor stops
new work; the former owner cannot overwrite the successor's checkpoint or budget.
External services are not transactional participants, so no exactly-once external
effect guarantee is added.

| Job state | Next action |
| --- | --- |
| Pending | Eligible for one fenced worker |
| Running | Current owner executes; only expired abandoned owners recover automatically |
| Waiting | Approval, reconciliation or session abandonment required; explicit resume afterward |
| Paused | Explicit queue resume |
| Failed | Inspect saved error/runtime intent; explicit resume using the same immutable input |
| Completed / Stopped | Terminal; idle workers never reclaim it |
| Abandoned | Operator permanently stopped scheduling; original runtime outcome remains unchanged |

`abandon` is an explicit scheduling retirement for an unavailable old host
contract or malformed host-only input. It requires the exact open job revision
and no live queue/runtime owner; an expired Running journal is eligible. The
cold CLI needs only SQL access. It records actor/note and releases queue capacity
without modifying runtime journals, session occupancy, spending or uncertain
effects. It does not claim that an external call failed or cancel a request
already executing at an external service. Abandoned scheduling cannot resume.
Old conversations can remain occupied until their existing controller receives
the required observed reconciliation/abandonment; use a new conversation for
independent work rather than rewriting history. After all open scheduling is
resolved or explicitly abandoned, a reviewed host-binding change is possible
while original unknown spending remains held.

There is no automatic retry of Failed/Waiting/Paused jobs. A worker killed during
a non-idempotent tool leaves the original approved call uncertain. A replacement
classifies the saved intent and waits for observed operator reconciliation; it
does not repeat the write. Lost/cancelled model responses retain conservative
generation reservations, even at zero declared API prices.

Control responses acknowledge **durable request delivery**, not instantaneous
completion. Workers observe control every 100ms when SQL is responsive; active
callbacks use the runtime's cooperative cancellation and unknown-effect rules.
A cancellation request can race a just-completed operation; inspect the actual
worker/runtime result. Pause stops at a durable boundary and can wait for an
active callback. Worker Ctrl+C requests pause; process death relies on lease
expiry. There is currently no bounded forced-shutdown CLI deadline: an active
callback may run to its configured timeout. A supervisor that hard-stops a worker
must preserve its journals and allow lease expiry before recovery.

Queue histories are bounded to 2048 events/1024 claims per job. New work is
refused before these limits exhaust outcome-recording capacity; oversized or
corrupt histories are never truncated or silently reset. Host-only malformed task
payloads become Failed without model dispatch. Generic SDK jobs outside the
Application task format require an explicit host/migration review, not edits to
their immutable payload. Current runtime association inspection is bounded to
8192 entries per job. Larger retained datasets require explicit future archival
or migration rather than deleting spending/uncertainty records.

## Reproduce and operate

```powershell
taskloom --config project.json queue
taskloom --config project.json queue-inspect run-hello
taskloom --config project.json queue-control run-hello 2 pause local-operator "review execution"
taskloom --config project.json queue-resume run-hello 3 local-operator "reviewed continuation"
taskloom --config project.json worker-once diagnostic-worker
cargo test --all-features --test database_queue --test app_queue
# Set the owned test PostgreSQL environment privately:
cargo test --all-features --test database_queue --test app_queue postgres -- --ignored
```

`worker-once` returns a job outcome or `null` when nothing can be claimed. Process
success means the outcome was acknowledged; inspect `state`, including Failed
and Stopped, rather than treating exit 0 as model success. Long-running `worker`
continues with other eligible jobs. Status, errors, audit actors, immutable input,
claim count and runtime associations are inspectable without model credentials.
New immutable inputs need new job/run identities; changing host contracts while
open jobs exist requires resolving them using their original contracts first.

For backup, stop API admission and workers, then verify no database-clock lease
is live. Back up all SQL tables/indexes together: runtime/budget, quota, queue
policy/jobs and runtime associations are one dataset. SQLite online backup and
PostgreSQL `pg_dump`/transactional `pg_restore` examples verify cold inspection
without model or connector credentials. Preserve the dataset UUID. Do not restore
partial journals or treat a backup as authority to repeat external effects.
Restore host secrets/configs/tool data separately, review credential revocations
and unresolved effects, and only then enable admission/workers.

```powershell
python examples/database/accept_queue.py target/NEW-native-queue --config target/native-generation-4b-config.json --taskloom target/debug/taskloom.exe --admin target/debug/examples/multiuser_host.exe --postgres-fixture target/OWNED-postgres --model-log target/OWNED-generation.log
python examples/database/queue_load.py target/NEW-load --taskloom target/debug/taskloom.exe --admin target/debug/examples/multiuser_host.exe --postgres-fixture target/OWNED-postgres
python examples/database/backup_acceptance.py target/NEW-queue-backup --kind queue --native target/NEW-native-queue --postgres-fixture target/OWNED-postgres --example target/debug/examples/multiuser_host.exe --taskloom target/debug/taskloom.exe
```

The bounded load uses four actual worker processes and the explicitly offline
fixture, 48 healthy jobs plus a paused/restarted control job per backend. It also
retires one never-executed job with unavailable model/MCP credentials to verify
the cold metadata path. It is
service/storage evidence, not native inference throughput. HTTP polling can miss
short active intervals; the report separately reconstructs running/open peaks
from persisted enqueue/claim/finish event clocks and retains all four actual
worker labels. Negative or inconsistent clock intervals are reported as failures.
Finite local results do not establish a production SLO or unlimited scalability.

The actual Qwen3-4B campaign separately observes eight native requests per backend
(seven reported usages, one unknown cancelled response), two overlapping worker
lifecycles, exact approval and actual process death during an fsynced MCP append.
Operator observation/reconciliation is labelled. Successful short role outputs
and lifecycle controls do not close the broader P0 research/semantic/long-task
quality gates. The retained first probe found unsupported MCP DELETE teardown;
the example connector now authenticates session deletion correctly. A contended
300ms heartbeat probe expired safely; the ordinary smoke uses one second and
native/process/load acceptance uses the ten-second production lease. No short-TTL
load guarantee is claimed. See `acceptance/p2-durable-queue-20261128.json` for raw
reports, failed probes, final source hashes and qualification of later diagnostics.

documents.title: Project generation quotas
documents.text:
# Project generation quotas

The opt-in SQL stores enforce one cumulative monetary cap and one outstanding
attempt cap per authenticated host-selected tenant/project. Every SQL run writer
uses the same project control lock, including Application/API/CLI, workflows,
sessions, memory extraction and direct `db.runs(scope)` calls. Creating another
pool or omitting a quota from a process configuration does not bypass a stored
policy. File journals do not gain distributed quotas.

This is generation accounting. Embedding has its separate ledger; generic tool
service charges remain separately unknown. A generation quota is not a durable
task queue, a rate limit or per-user billing. Separate
[queue/worker and bounded load evidence](durable-queue.md) covers those service
operations; broad native quality remains in P0.

## Configure explicitly

```rust,no_run
use taskloom::runtime::database::*;
# async fn example() -> Result<(), taskloom::runtime::RuntimeError> {
let db = SqlDatabase::sqlite("service.sqlite", DatabaseOptions::default()).await?;
db.migrate().await?;
let project = DatabaseNamespace::new("tenant-a", "project-a")?;
let quota = db.generation_quota(project);
let current = quota.snapshot().await?;
quota.configure(Some(GenerationQuota {
    currency: "USD".into(), max_cost_micros: 2_000_000,
    max_outstanding_attempts: 4,
}), current.policy_revision, "local-admin", "explicit reviewed USD generation cap").await?;
db.close().await;
# Ok(()) }
```

Only trusted administration exposes `configure`; it is not a model tool or a
public HTTP mutation. The source example supplies local administration without
model/connector credentials:

```powershell
cargo build --all-features --example multiuser_host
# Resolve TASKLOOM_DATABASE_URL privately on this host; never print its value.
target/debug/examples/multiuser_host quota-get tenant-a project-a
# policy.json: {"currency":"USD","max_cost_micros":2000000,"max_outstanding_attempts":4}
target/debug/examples/multiuser_host quota-set tenant-a project-a policy.json 0 local-admin "explicit reviewed cap"
```

Policy changes require the exact `policy_revision`, operator and a bounded audit
note. Ordinary usage changes advance `revision` without invalidating policy CAS.
The database supplies audit time. At most 1024 policy changes are retained; the
store refuses further changes rather than silently truncating audit history.

Prices in the model gateway must use the declared currency; this is an explicit
host attestation, not conversion or provider-billing verification. Currency is
immutable after initialization, including while enforcement is disabled.
Custom trusted model adapters must obey `RunBudget::requires_cost_ceiling()`,
reserve a conservative known ceiling through `reserve_before_dispatch` for
every retry/fallback and settle only with known usage. The built-in gateway does
this. **All SQL runs require known prices even without an individual run cap or
an active project quota**, closing the race with later quota configuration.
Lease/journal wrappers must forward `requires_cost_ceiling`; defaults preserve
compatibility for existing file/non-expiring implementations.

## Accounting and recovery

Admission and the run's reservation journal commit in the same transaction,
before provider dispatch. The lock order is runtime ownership, project quota,
then accounting records. Administrator imports lock the project control row
and read committed journals without taking runtime leases. PostgreSQL row locks
and SQLite's immediate writer serialize competing processes.

Held cost is `committed_micros + in_flight_micros`. Uncertain cost is already
included in committed and is not counted twice. Outstanding attempts are
`in_flight_attempts + uncertain_attempts`: zero-priced requests occupy slots.
Known settlement releases only that attempt's slot. A lost response or killed
process retains its ceiling and slot; converting in-flight into uncertain does
not free capacity. The ledger does not silently refund or erase uncertain work.

A quota `Budget` refusal means a transaction was rolled back and no dispatch
was admitted. The runtime removes only the refused reservation and records the
budget stop without inventing uncertain fees. Other storage/commit failures
remain ambiguous and retain conservative uncertainty. Reservation registration
is serialized per run; provider execution can still overlap.

Already incurred cost is saved even if it exceeds the project cap or its
reservation. Such a checkpoint sets a sticky `overrun` marker and stops fresh
admission. A trusted administrator can explicitly review/reconfigure the policy
when retained usage fits. Increasing an outstanding cap permits recovery/new
work while retaining the original unknown attempt. It cannot change a finished
run's terminal result or replay an uncertain external write.

An absent/unconfigured scope reports `usage: null`, meaning historical spending
is uninitialized. First configuration imports the newest checkpoint/reservation
generation for **every** existing run, including orphan reservation journals,
under the same project lock. Equal generations require identical budgets;
committed/uncertain amounts cannot decrease. The bounded import streams up to
100000 run/journal rows and 64MiB and refuses oversized/corrupt histories; it
does not use the UI's truncated listing or reset history. Each run gets a small
accounting record. Unconfigured SDK users do not trigger a historical scan.

Disabling enforcement requires an explicit `configure(None, ...)` (CLI JSON
`null`). Accounting continues so reenabling cannot reset spending. There is no
automatic calendar reset, historical currency conversion, pruning/refund API or
renewable rate window in this increment.

## Schema-v2 migration

Schema v2 introduced the generation-quota barrier. The current
`SqlDatabase::migrate` / `taskloom database-migrate` creates schema v3 or upgrades
v1/v2 in one transaction, including queue indexes/ownership. Stop all old hosts and workers first. Upgrade
refuses while any database-clock lease is live; PostgreSQL also locks the lease
table during the version barrier. Dataset UUID and existing version-1 JSON
envelopes/runtime checkpoints are preserved. Unknown versions and downgrades are
refused. Back up the complete database before upgrading and restore the complete
backup with its matching binary if rollback is required.

Old v1 binaries do not participate in quota enforcement. Their schema/ownership
checks fail after the barrier; old v2 binaries also lack queue enforcement.
New SQL acquisition, renewal, ownership and commit checks require
`DATABASE_SCHEMA_VERSION` (3). Historical v2 acceptance below remains v2 evidence.
Opening an Application does not run migrations. Re-run the explicit migration
on the intended database; do not create an empty replacement and call it migrated.

The schema changes neither `AgentTask`, minimal default features, Rust 1.86 nor
the file journal format. The added default trait methods preserve source
compatibility for existing stores; wrappers around SQL must forward them.

## Reproduce controls

```powershell
cargo test --all-features --test database_quota
# Owned local PostgreSQL only; resolve its private URL into the named env.
cargo test --all-features --test database_quota postgres_project_quota_atomic_admission_and_accounting -- --ignored --exact
cargo build --all-features --bin taskloom --example multiuser_host
python examples/database/accept_quota.py target/NEW-quota-native --config target/native-generation-4b-config.json --taskloom target/debug/taskloom.exe --admin target/debug/examples/multiuser_host.exe --postgres-fixture target/OWNED-postgres --model-log target/OWNED-generation.log
python examples/database/backup_acceptance.py target/NEW-quota-backup --native target/NEW-quota-native --postgres-fixture target/OWNED-postgres --example target/debug/examples/multiuser_host.exe --taskloom target/debug/taskloom.exe --kind quota
# Upgrade copies of retained v1 native data, never the original artifacts:
python examples/database/accept_quota_migration.py target/NEW-quota-migration --sqlite-v1 target/V1-native/application.sqlite --postgres-v1-dump target/V1-backup/application.dump --postgres-fixture target/OWNED-postgres --native-campaign target/V1-native --admin target/debug/examples/multiuser_host.exe
```

The native harness requires explicitly zero-priced loopback inference, uses
separate CLI/admin processes, observes a real native request before killing its
own child, waits the production ten-second lease, retains uncertainty and tests
explicit quota review plus cold terminal reentry. Failed probes and actual
acceptance results are recorded separately; fixture tests are not model quality,
native cost/latency rankings or service-worker/load evidence.

2026-11-28 acceptance: each real database passed ten native/separate-process
controls, observing two real generation requests (one interrupted with unknown
response usage). Both retained the original uncertain slot after known new-run
settlement. Quiescent SQLite online backup and PostgreSQL transactional restore
passed three additional controls. Copies of the actual preceding schema-v1
native databases passed four migration/import controls: all 31 SQLite and 146
PostgreSQL records remained byte-identical across the version barrier, and the
explicit native scopes imported their latest seven/eight run budgets. The
PostgreSQL dump also contains separately labelled fixture scopes; those are not
native API costs. See `acceptance/p2-generation-quota-20261128.json`.

Retained harness faults include missing required RunLimits fields before any
native dispatch, a Windows default-text-codec failure reading Unicode SQL data,
and an intermediate migration probe that automatically selected a fixture scope.
The final migration probe selects the recorded native scope explicitly. These
do not become successful native trials or evidence of old-binary dispatch/rolling
upgrade safety; operators must quiesce old hosts before migration.

# Reviewed cross-session memory

Enable `runtime` for the SDK and `app` for the local API/CLI. Memory is opt-in
and separate from conversation history, the knowledge corpus and model spending.
The minimal default feature set and typed `AgentTask` API are unchanged.

## Host configuration and access

Add this fragment to a complete application configuration:

```json
{
  "memory": {
    "scope": {"tenant":"local", "project":"assistant", "owner":"alice"},
    "actor": "local-operator",
    "curate": true,
    "recall": {"max_items":8, "max_bytes":16384, "include_preferences":true}
  }
}
```

The host chooses this scope and authenticated actor. API/model input cannot
select a tenant, project, owner, actor or curator grant. `curate` defaults to
false; readers can inspect/recall their namespace but cannot extract, review,
edit or forget. Memory is disabled when the optional property is absent.
Extraction additionally requires `limits.max_cost_micros` and explicit prices
for the configured model. No extraction happens automatically after a chat.

For the SDK, construct `MemoryAccess::reader` or `MemoryAccess::curator` only
after authenticating and authorizing the caller. The type deliberately cannot
be deserialized. `MemoryManager` takes this access object, with no second
caller-selected scope. `MemoryStore` is a trusted persistence interface;
calling its raw methods is not an authorization API. Protect its filesystem.

The current local application still has one bearer-authenticated operator.
Its memory namespace isolation does **not** provide multi-user authorization
for sessions, runs or the rest of the application. P2's authenticated service
scope and database work remain separate delivery gates.

## Extraction and review

Choose a successful, closed session turn. The host loads that session and
selects its actual User message. Assistant/tool replies, open/failed turns and
previously recalled memory are ineligible sources. For a memory-aware turn,
only its original `request` field is eligible; injected records never become
fresh user testimony.

The configured native model proposes up to sixteen `{kind,key,value,quote}`
records. `kind` is `fact` or `preference`; `key` is a bounded lowercase semantic
slot such as `language` or `project.runtime`. The host supplies source session,
turn/run/message identity and fingerprints, and checks the quote verbatim.
Model output cannot supply ownership or permission fields. The extraction
child has no tools, uses exact JSON/schema validation, reserves its model
spending durably and retains failed or uncertain attempts under normal rules.

All proposals begin as **candidates**. Only explicit host/operator review
activates them. An exact quote establishes provenance, not that the proposed
value follows from it. Review values and their sources before accepting; a
wrong statement or sensitive value can still be proposed by a model. This is
not a general secret detector or factual-truth verifier.

Slots use exact `(kind,key)` identity. A second candidate for an occupied slot
cannot become active without `replace:true`; replacement retains the previous
version as superseded. There is no automatic semantic deduplication between
`language`, `reply.language` and `preferred_language`. Inspect such proposals
and reject inappropriate aliases; do not assume model-selected keys are a
canonical ontology. Editing an active value creates a new active version
linked to the previous version and the operator's note. Its original source
quote remains provenance of the earlier proposal, not proof of the edit.

## API and CLI

All HTTP routes below are under `/api` with the existing bearer authentication.
JSON requests deny unknown identity/grant fields. Every mutation requires the
exact current `expected_revision`; conflicts require inspection, not a force
overwrite or silent model retry.

| Operation | API | CLI |
|---|---|---|
| Export records, versions, sources and audit hashes | `GET /memory` | `memory` |
| Bounded recall | `POST /memory/recall` with `{"text":"project runtime"}` | `memory-recall "project runtime"` |
| Explicit model extraction | `POST /memory/extract` | `memory-extract extract.json` |
| Accept/reject a candidate | `POST /memory/review` | `memory-review review.json` |
| Edit an active value | `POST /memory/edit` | `memory-edit edit.json` |
| Forget a slot and all its versions | `POST /memory/forget` | `memory-forget forget.json` |
| Start a turn with frozen recall | `POST /sessions/{id}/memory-turns` | SDK/API |

Example request files, used with `taskloom --config local-provider.json COMMAND`:

```json
{"expected_revision":0,"session_id":"source","turn_id":"one","request_id":"learn-source"}
```

```json
{"expected_revision":1,"id":"actual-candidate-hash","accept":true,"replace":false,"note":"checked against the user's source statement"}
```

```json
{"expected_revision":2,"id":"actual-active-hash","value":"Chinese","note":"owner clarified the preference"}
```

```json
{"expected_revision":3,"kind":"preference","key":"language"}
```

Create the destination session through `POST /sessions` as usual. Its
`memory-turns` body is the ordinary `{turn_id,prompt}` shape. Ordinary `turns`
continues to omit memory. The memory-aware route freezes query, namespace,
revision and source-linked hits in a clearly labelled **User-data** JSON
envelope with a separate original `request`. It changes neither the system
prefix nor tools/grants. Prompt-like memory content cannot grant a tool. The
envelope is visible in the archived transcript and durable input; clients can
render its `request` separately. Reentering the same turn reuses this envelope
even if memory changed. A different original request or scope is rejected.

Recall is local lexical overlap using the existing Unicode tokenizer. Explicitly
reviewed preferences can also be included without overlap; turn this off for
strict query-only recall. Candidate/rejected/superseded records are excluded.
Item/serialized-byte limits are enforced; oversized higher-ranked records are
reported and lower-ranked fitting records may still be returned. Inspect
`matched_terms`, `preference`, `omitted` and `skipped_oversize`. This is not an
embedding index or a promise of semantic recall across languages/paraphrases.

CLI export, recall, review, edit and forget operate without loading generation
or MCP credentials. CLI extraction loads only the configured generation model;
it does not contact configured MCP services or offer tools. SDK usage:

```rust,no_run
use taskloom::runtime::memory::*;
# async fn example() -> Result<(),taskloom::runtime::RuntimeError> {
let store = FileMemoryStore::new("state/memory");
let access = MemoryAccess::reader(MemoryScope {
    tenant:"local".into(), project:"assistant".into(), owner:"alice".into()
}, "authenticated-actor")?;
let manager = MemoryManager::new(&store);
let recalled = manager.recall(&access, "project runtime", &MemoryRecallPolicy::default()).await?;
// Pass a curator access object for review/edit/forget; never derive it from
// the model's answer. Extraction uses an explicitly bounded AgentLoop/RunStore.
println!("{} source-linked memories", recalled.hits.len());
# Ok(()) }
```

## Recovery, erasure and migration

Version-1 file snapshots live under `state_dir/memory/<scope-hash>.memory.json`.
Writes take per-scope OS locks, verify CAS/audit prefixes, flush a temporary file
and atomically replace the previous snapshot. Reads fail on corruption; they
do not silently reset state. Limits are 16 MiB, 4096 records, 16,384 forgotten
source bindings and 20,000 audit events. Admission also reserves 2 KiB, one
possible tombstone and one possible erasure event per retained record, so
administrative forgetting is not stranded by an admitted full snapshot.
A limit refuses the operation without
replacing the valid snapshot. Export/backup before planned migration; retain
the scope and revisions when implementing another `MemoryStore`.

Extraction request IDs bind a scope and the exact selected input to a durable
`memory-<hash>` child. Repeating a completed request with a fresh inspected
memory revision reuses its answer without another model request. If memory CAS
or capacity fails after generation, the completed extraction run stays in the
run store; inspect it and retry the **same request ID**, with the correct
revision/configuration. Do not silently mint a new paid request. Interrupting
generation preserves its spending uncertainty; normal interrupted-model
recovery can admit a further attempt within the original cap. API admission
is released even if the extraction caller drops its future.

Forgetting physically removes every candidate/current/superseded/rejected
version of that slot from the memory snapshot. It retains only audit record
hashes and source-binding tombstones, preventing an old extraction of that same
source/slot from resurrecting the value, even if a later extractor proposes
different wording. A genuinely new user statement can propose the slot again.
This is memory-store erasure, not secure disk wiping or deletion of source
sessions, completed extraction runs, already frozen turn inputs, exports or
external backups. Those histories remain independently retained. New recalls
exclude forgotten records; old frozen inputs remain reproducible.

No automatic legacy-history import or schema conversion runs on upgrade. Absent
`memory` preserves previous application behavior, session format and durable
configuration fingerprints. Direct `AppConfig` struct literals need the new
optional field or `..Default::default()`.

## Reproducible acceptance

```powershell
cargo test --locked --all-features --test agent_memory --test app_memory
python examples/benchmarks/native_memory.py target/native-memory-new --config local-provider.json --taskloom target/debug/taskloom.exe
```

The tests explicitly label model fixtures and cover CAS/isolation, source
checks, bounded Unicode/negative recall, permission injection, CRUD/restart,
frozen inputs, no resurrection, model-spend uncertainty and credential-free
CLI management. The native example calls only an explicitly zero-priced
loopback API. It retains model proposals unchanged, curates only prelabelled
source-supported values and tests actual new-session use, conflicts, CLI edits,
host restarts and erasure. `acceptance/p1-memory-20261128.json` records results
and limitations; this visible small set is not a broad extraction benchmark.

documents.text:
# Data-only skills, templates and connectors

The `runtime` SDK and optional `app` host support installable, content-pinned
skill packages. They contain UTF-8 guidance, typed role/output contracts,
workflow templates and connector configuration examples. Installation stores
inert JSON objects: it does not execute scripts, register a tool, start a
service, read a declared credential or grant a permission.

## Package format and authoring

Examples live in `examples/skills/`:

| Package | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `evidence-base` | Reusable evidence and permission guidance dependency |
| `research-brief` | Local corpus research role and cited source-summary template |
| `connector-notes` | Repository metadata, note-status and approved note-append templates |

Each directory has a root `skill.json`. Format 1 declares name, exact version,
description, SHA-256 for every asset, exact dependency `{name,version,digest}`
pins, tool effects/permissions, required credential **names**, roles, templates
and optional connector-example metadata. Names use lowercase ASCII letters,
digits and hyphens; versions are exact canonical `major.minor.patch` integer
triples. Ranges, prereleases, network URLs, install hooks and implicit dependency
downloads are unavailable in this format.

Asset paths are portable relative paths. Roles select an instruction asset,
optional assets from explicitly pinned direct dependencies, declared tool names
and a `WorkflowOutput` contract. Template DAGs/PEER specs refer to local roles;
the host mounts them under its own prefix. Template input is schema-validated
before workflow persistence or model dispatch. Content includes do not expand
directives found inside text. Connector JSON is documentation, never applied
automatically to the host configuration.

Create deterministic plain POSIX USTAR archives from trusted authoring sources:

```powershell
python examples/skills/pack.py examples/skills/evidence-base target/evidence-base.tar
python examples/skills/pack.py examples/skills/research-brief target/research-brief.tar
python examples/skills/pack.py examples/skills/connector-notes target/connector-notes.tar
```

The helper creates a new archive only and checks declared asset hashes. Preserve
LF content; the repository attributes pin these source files to LF on Windows.
After an intentional asset edit, update its manifest hash and publish a new
version. Updating a dependency requires its new exact pin. The dependency pin in
the shipped research example matches the shipped evidence-base package.

The Rust reader independently enforces an 8 MiB transport limit, at most 128
assets/256 entries, 256 KiB per entry, 4 MiB total content and a 128 KiB manifest.
It accepts uncompressed USTAR regular files/directories and rejects links,
devices, GNU/PAX extensions, gzip/zip, traversal, absolute/drive/stream paths,
reserved Windows names, case collisions, malformed checksums, nonzero padding,
duplicate entries and ambiguous trailing bytes. Assets become in-memory strings
and a single digest-addressed JSON object; no archive path is extracted to disk.
Combined role guidance is capped at 128 KiB. Dependency resolution is bounded
to 32 packages/16 MiB, with a depth guard.

The package digest is the format-1 normalized manifest/assets identity, not the
tar byte hash or a publisher signature. Formatting/default serialization is
normalized; all declared content and dependencies are bound. Review provenance
and contents before granting a package access. Hashes establish identity and
integrity, not publisher trust or factual quality.

## Install, inspect and retire

```powershell
taskloom --config host.json skills
taskloom --config host.json skill-install target/evidence-base.tar 0
taskloom --config host.json skill-install target/research-brief.tar 1
taskloom --config host.json skill-install target/connector-notes.tar 2
```

The final argument is the exact current catalog revision. Install dependencies
first. The output includes the exact `package` pin and `activated:false`.
These commands do not initialize model/MCP services or load their credentials.
Write the bare `{name,version,digest}` object to `pin.json` to inspect or retire:

```powershell
taskloom --config host.json skill-inspect pin.json
taskloom --config host.json skill-retire pin.json 3
```

Catalog/object writes use a catalog OS lock, CAS, flushed atomic replacement and
immutable content objects under `state_dir/skills`. A same-version/different-
content install is refused, even after retirement. Identical reinstalls are
idempotent after inspecting the current revision. An interrupted object write
cannot create an activated package; retry the same archive and current catalog
revision. Corrupt catalogs/objects fail rather than silently resetting. Limits
are 256 known versions and 20,000 audit events, with retirement-event headroom.
Keep this directory trusted and back up catalog plus objects together.

Retirement removes the package from new activation/selection. Installed
dependents must be retired first; there is no implicit cascade. Objects remain
for audit and explicit recovery pins. An already loaded application keeps its
frozen snapshot; stop/reconfigure/restart it to change admissions. Retirement
is not a running-process kill or deletion of old run history.

## Host activation and durable identity

Host configuration opts in separately, using the verified install pin:

```json
{
  "skills": [{
    "package": {"name":"research-brief", "version":"1.0.0", "digest":"COPY_THE_EXACT_INSTALLED_DIGEST"},
    "mount": "research",
    "mode": "active",
    "grant": {"tools":["knowledge_search"], "permissions":["knowledge:read"], "credentials":[]}
  }]
}
```

This is a fragment, not a complete provider configuration. The research host
must enable knowledge access and set an explicit generation ceiling for output
repairs. Mount prefixes are 1–14 lowercase ASCII letters/digits/hyphens;
mounted role names cannot collide with host roles or other mounts.

Every dependency's tool requirements must match the host's actual registered
tool effects and complete permission sets. Grants must be subsets of the
original host policy. Required credential names need both explicit package
grants and a host-configured provider/service name; package text never receives
the environment values. Packages cannot downgrade a write to a read, define a
service endpoint for the host, enlarge a tool policy, waive exact approval,
remove spending ceilings or silently retry an uncertain effect. Tool-service
and embedding charges retain their separate host boundaries.

New durable skill children freeze root package, transitive pins, local role and
grant identity in `RunConfig.skill_binding`, alongside the existing exact tool
definitions, limits and approval policy. Workflow task contracts also freeze
guidance and output schema. Changing package/version/content/dependencies or
grants cannot approve or resume an old operation. Keep its original pin/config.
The original contracts remain necessary for approval and recovery; removing a
tool or changing its definition does not invent permission to replay it.

For an explicitly retired original package, `mode:"recovery_only"` allows a
host to restore its exact contracts. The app hides its templates and refuses
new workflows using those roles, while allowing old workflows to resume.
Use a separate recovery configuration rather than silently substituting the new
version. The SDK exposes mode on `ActivatedSkill`; SDK hosts must enforce
start/resume admission when using its low-level `configure_role` builder.
Host authentication/authorization remains the caller's responsibility.

`GET /api/templates` lists active templates; `GET /api/roles` includes compiled
role contracts. `POST /api/templates/{mount}/{template}/runs` accepts only
`{id,input,limits}` and creates an ordinary persisted workflow. It cannot accept
a caller-provided grant, role implementation or package. Inspect, approve,
pause/resume and reconcile it through the existing workflow/node routes.

## Working MCP connector source

`connector_service.py` is an explicitly started loopback-only MCP HTTP service:

```powershell
python examples/skills/connector_service.py --notes target/example-notes --repository seriable/taskloom
```

Configure `TASKLOOM_EXAMPLE_CONNECTOR_TOKEN` in the process environment first
(at least sixteen characters; no need to send its value to chat). The connector
example JSON shows the explicit host endpoint, namespace, token environment
and three bindings. Grant that credential name when activating connector-notes.
No service is started by installing it. A tool-calling model is needed to run
its templates; the offline demonstration is not a substitute for native evidence.

The repository identity is a server startup argument, not model input. Metadata
uses one bounded HTTPS request to public `api.github.com`, no environment proxy,
no redirects, no automatic retries and a twenty-request process cap. Private
access requires a separately supplied `--github-token-env`; ambient credentials
are never discovered. Public REST reads have an explicit zero API price in the
example; rate/response/failure observations are retained separately from model
charges. The service is a bounded example, not a production GitHub integration.

Notes use an owned directory, bounded exact text and a flushed append. The tool
is explicitly **non-idempotent**; JSON-RPC IDs do not deduplicate writes. Optional
`--fail-after-append-once` persists a note and then loses the response to exercise
reconciliation. Inspect `notes_status` and the external record before an operator
records the observed result. Never turn response loss into an automatic append
retry. The native harness performs these operator actions explicitly and labels
them separately from model generation. Repository/store identities participate
in tool descriptions, so changing them changes the frozen tool contract.

## Migration and acceptance

No automatic package import or activation occurs on upgrade. Empty `skills`
and absent `skill_binding` serialize without new fields, preserving previous
configuration fingerprints. Direct `AppConfig`/`RunConfig` literals need the new
field or an applicable default update. The typed task API, default features,
dependency set and Rust 1.86 requirement are unchanged. Packages are guidance
data; they do not install Rust/Python dependencies or sandbox an ordinary host
tool. Future package format changes must preserve format-1 digest semantics or
use a new format rather than silently rewriting old identities.

```powershell
cargo test --locked --all-features --test agent_skills --test app_skills
python examples/benchmarks/native_skills.py target/native-skills-new --config local-provider.json --taskloom target/debug/taskloom.exe
```

The automatic tests use explicitly labelled model fixtures for control,
permission, archive and approval/restart behavior. The native campaign actually
installs the example archives without model credentials, starts the MCP service,
calls the configured zero-priced local model, reads live GitHub data, appends to
the filesystem and reconciles a real lost response across a host restart and
package retirement. The cited research template's model failure is retained;
neither package installation nor passing connector cases establishes general
research quality. See `acceptance/p1-skills-20261128.json` for transcripts,
failures, prices, checks and source/artifact identities. P0-P2 is unfinished.

An explicit new source version, `examples/skills/research-located`, publishes
the **research-brief 1.1.0** manifest with `located_cited_report`. It depends on
the unchanged evidence-base 1.0.0. Its first native probe still failed due to
wrong document identity, absent ordinal markers and source-prefixed quotations;
the host rejected these outputs. A second probe with clarified role guidance
and JSON-formatted locator feedback passed all four templates and thirteen
control checks. The research answer quoted the actual approval document and
retained its original ordinal-form model JSON alongside explicit host mappings.
Prompts, package digest and output format changed; this is a new acceptance
campaign, not a controlled score improvement over 1.0.0.

```powershell
python examples/benchmarks/native_skills.py target/native-skills-located --config local-provider.json --taskloom target/debug/taskloom.exe --research-package research-located
```

Version 1.0.0's source and failed evidence are unchanged. Select 1.1.0 for new
runs only, keeping the original package/configuration for any old recovery.
The declared bounded source examples now have native execution evidence;
general research quality, larger collaboration, registry trust and multi-user
authorization are separate gates. See `final-output.md` and
`acceptance/p0-locators-20261128.json` for exact conditions and retained failures.

documents.text:
# Journal diagnostics and explicit OpenTelemetry export

`runtime::observability` projects **validated saved journals** into a correlated
trace. It performs no model, embedding or tool calls. There is no process-global
subscriber, automatic uploader, implicit `OTEL_*` environment discovery or
send-on-drop behavior. Network export requires the optional `telemetry` feature;
the application feature includes it, while default features remain empty.

## Trace and time semantics

`TraceSnapshot::run`, `workflow` and `session` build run or parent traces.
Workflow/node/durable-run and session/turn/durable-run relationships come from
persisted references and exact initial-input bindings. Closed session children
also match the recorded report fingerprint. Unreferenced, duplicate or mismatched
children fail; absent children are counted. Active durable children can be found
through their frozen node context before an outcome returns to the parent.
Reads of separate records are individually atomic, **not** a cross-record
transaction or a guarantee that a live parent and child were read simultaneously.

Stable SHA-256-derived IDs use a trusted host namespace and logical identities.
Revisions change the source revision key, not existing trace/span identities.
Changing the namespace changes IDs. The application defaults to a namespace
derived from its absolute state root; set an explicit namespace before moving
journals if continuity across deployment paths matters. These hashes provide
correlation and pseudonymization, not cryptographic storage authentication.

Spans cover workflows, nodes, individual dispatches, durable runs, model
decisions, tool attempts, retrieval, approval waits, operator reconciliation and
output validation. A model decision can contain gateway HTTP retries; the native
usage request count is a different quantity. A node can dispatch repeatedly to
the **same** durable child without repeating an uncertain external effect.
Child usage is counted once, not again as parent workflow usage.

New managed children persist a host-owned `TraceBinding` before their first
checkpoint. Independently inspecting such a child uses the same trace, global
root, run and descendant span IDs as inspecting its workflow/session. The
binding is outside model input and execution configuration, changes no grants,
and is immutable across checkpoint revisions, including cancellation. A model
cannot create it through a prompt. SDK callers may attach an exact managed
identity with `DurableAgent::with_trace_binding`; invalid child IDs or workflow
input bindings fail before the initial budget journal is created.

Child-only views have `selected_span_id` pointing at the real run and two
`context_only` ancestor references. References have unknown outcome, no clocks
and no asserted completion: they are omitted from OTLP as `omitted_context`,
separately from actually open or missing-clock observations. Inspect the owning
parent for its current observed state. These projections do not install a live
subscriber or inject W3C headers into external services.

New `RunEvent` and `WorkflowEvent` records include optional `unix_ms`. Relative
elapsed time still drives the existing execution limits; wall time never changes
approval, budget or recovery admission. The OTLP projection uses actual recorded
Unix times, including downtime between parent/run start and completion. Active
elapsed time is a separate attribute and may exclude operator/offline waits.
Missing, backwards or overflowing wall clocks stay visible and are omitted from
trace export; they are never synthesized from relative durations. Open spans are
not exported as completed. Sessions have no close operation, so their root stays
open; completed turns/runs can be exported with that still-open parent ID.

A stopped uncertain tool span retains its historical uncertainty even after
successful reconciliation; the separate recovery span records the bounded
`record_result`, `retry_safe` or `abort` action. It does not export the actor,
note or observed result. Output-rejection/validation spans retain repair history.
Span status and safe stage codes distinguish model, tool, output-contract,
authorization, context, storage, generation-budget and recovery outcomes.

## Metrics, retrieval and billing

Metrics describe the selected scope's saved journal: model decisions, native
usage requests/tokens, tool attempts/errors, recovered models, output checks,
omitted context messages, retrievals, empty recalls and skipped oversized chunks.
OTLP exports up to eighteen **gauges**, not process-wide totals, deltas or a cross-run
latency ranking. Re-exporting snapshots can resend the same completed span IDs;
the receipt/revision key permits host-side tracking, but exporter delivery is not
exactly once. No automatic retry hides an uncertain receiver outcome.
Gauges bind both `taskloom.trace_id` and `taskloom.selected_span_id`. A parent
scope includes its children; a child scope contains only that run. Do not sum
overlapping scopes or treat repeated snapshot observations as incremental work.
Completeness and usage-reporting flags accompany the observations. Missing child
records suppress generation gauges; unreported provider usage suppresses token
and request gauges. Missing data does not become a zero-valued measurement.
Local JSON retains recorded subtotals with those explicit validity flags.

Generation usage and spending come from saved run checkpoints. While a model
request is live, its independently persisted spending-reservation journal can
be newer; these metrics are **not a live invoice** or a replacement for admission
accounting. The existing budget controller still persists reservations before
paid dispatch. Generation micro-units use the configured price-table currency.
Committed generation amounts already include uncertain-attempt ceilings; do not
add the uncertainty field again. In-flight reservations remain separate.
Embedding remains in its independent host ledger (`index-status` / `/retrieval`);
per-run embedding allocation is unavailable here. Generic tools do not report
service billing. Those two attributed cost fields are `null`, never assumed zero.
An explicit zero-priced connector example does not make arbitrary tools free.

Saved retrieval diagnostics expose revision, returned/skipped counts and scores.
Local inspection also shows exact document/chunk IDs, titles and byte ranges to
identify problematic recall without repeating a paid query. Body quotes, source
URIs and tool arguments are not added to this view. The exporter **never** sends
these local hit records: its separate allowlist admits only static names,
pseudonymous IDs, validated statuses, booleans and numerical attributes. Tests
check that prompts, model/tool names, arguments, answers and source contents do
not enter OTLP. An SDK caller adding an unrecognized span attribute gets an error.

## Application configuration and operations

No `observability` setting is needed for local inspection. To explicitly enable
export operations, add this host-owned config fragment:

```json
{
  "observability": {
    "namespace": "my-project-development",
    "otlp": {
      "endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:4318",
      "service_name": "taskloom",
      "bearer_env": null,
      "timeout_ms": 10000,
      "max_in_flight": 2,
      "max_payload_bytes": 2097152
    }
  }
}
```

Configuring a destination constructs an inert HTTP client; **only an explicit
export operation sends data**. `bearer_env` names an optional host environment
containing a bearer token, resolved when constructing the exporter. Never put
the token value in configuration or model input. The receiver URL cannot contain
credentials, query parameters or a fragment. HTTP is restricted to loopback;
other destinations require HTTPS. No ambient proxy or redirect is followed.
The service name is an explicitly exported host label; choose a nonsecret name.

```powershell
taskloom --config taskloom.json diagnostics workflow research-job
taskloom --config taskloom.json trace-export workflow research-job REVISION_KEY EXPORT_BINDING
```

`diagnostics` accepts `run`, `workflow` or `session` and executes before model,
MCP and exporter initialization. It works with service credentials removed.
Use the displayed source revision key and export binding for `trace-export`.
They bind the read journals and configured destination/options; changed inputs
require inspecting again. These read-only commands never rewind live stores.

Authenticated API equivalents are `GET /api/diagnostics/{kind}/{id}` and
`POST /api/diagnostics/{kind}/{id}/export` with exactly
`{source_revision_key,export_binding}`. The request cannot supply a destination,
headers or a model/tool implementation. Changed revisions or export settings
return 409 before sending. The UI shows parent IDs, clocks, outcomes, metrics,
error stages and retrieval details, and displays the configured destination
before enabling its explicit export button. Ordinary viewing does not export.
This is the existing single-operator bearer host, not P2 multi-user authorization.

The separate comparison view reads two version-1 Taskloom `BenchmarkReport`
files **locally**. It shows case outcomes, failures, recorded ledgers and declared
condition differences. Fixture/offline ledgers do not measure actual API/chat
fees, and their wall time is integration time. Imported content is not attested;
matching labels do not establish equal prompts, prices, hardware or independent
claim support. The view remains descriptive and does not infer leadership or
latency rankings. Other campaign schemas, including the current standalone
LangGraph adapter report, need an explicit adapter and are rejected visibly.
Each selected file is bounded to 4 MiB and 256 cases; select a narrower campaign
when a report exceeds those UI limits.

## Bounds, shutdown and error behavior

SDK snapshots accept at most 4,096 spans, 32,768 events per record and 256 child
runs. Application inspection caps a record at 16 MiB and child records at 64 MiB
combined. Larger histories require selecting narrower runs. Export defaults to
two in-flight calls and 2 MiB per signal payload. A full semaphore rejects the
operation before allocating payload buffers; there is no unbounded queue.
Responses are capped at 16 KiB, each HTTP attempt has a timeout, and both trace
and metric outcomes appear separately in the receipt. HTTP errors, OTLP partial
acceptance, invalid responses and acceptance-unknown timeouts are not successes.
Oversized payloads fail before either signal is sent. No automatic retry occurs.

`OtlpHttpExporter::shutdown` refuses new work and waits up to its configured
timeout for admitted operations. On timeout it reports remaining work; callers
still own those futures, which retain their own request deadlines. There are no
exporter-created background workers to leak. Application shutdown uses this
method. A dropped/cancelled network future may have been accepted remotely;
repeat export is an explicit host decision, not an exactly-once guarantee.

## Migration and reproducible acceptance

Missing `unix_ms` deserializes to `None` and serializes without the new field,
preserving old journal/report hashes and old closed-session bindings. No config,
approval input or model transcript is migrated or changed. Old records remain
locally diagnosable but have no fabricated OTLP trace timing. Rust struct literals
for `RunEvent`/`WorkflowEvent` must add `unix_ms`; direct `AppConfig` literals need
the new optional `observability` field or a default update. `AgentTask` API,
minimal default features and Rust 1.86 remain supported. There are no new crates.

Missing `RunState.trace_binding` remains absent when serialized. Old unbound
children resume without backfill and retain their original input/report hashes;
their standalone view still has a standalone trace. Parent inspection continues
to join them from its verified persisted references. No implicit scan, parent
inference from model text or historical ID rewrite is performed. New direct
`RunState` literals must supply `trace_binding: None` or an exact host binding.
Custom `RunLease` backends must preserve the original binding, including legacy
`None`, as the file store does. A strict resume with conflicting existing host
binding fails; administrative cancellation can still resolve the original run.

```powershell
cargo test --locked --all-features --test agent_observability
python examples/observability/download_collector.py target/collector-pinned
target/collector-pinned/otelcol.exe --config target/collector-loopback.yaml
python examples/benchmarks/native_skills.py target/native-observability --config local-native-otlp.json --taskloom target/debug/taskloom.exe --research-package research-located
python examples/observability/accept_native.py target/native-observability --taskloom target/debug/taskloom.exe --collector-log target/collector.log
python examples/observability/accept_sessions.py target/native-session-traces --config local-native-otlp.json --taskloom target/debug/taskloom.exe --collector-log target/collector.log
```

See `examples/observability/README.md` for loopback receiver setup and versions,
and `acceptance/p1-observability-20261128.json` for raw native evidence, actual
Collector output, browser observations, failures and check boundaries. The later
`acceptance/p1-trace-binding-20261128.json` records fresh native workflow/session
parent binding, cold CLI/API continuity, actual receiver acceptance and failed
diagnostic-ID probes before the fix. This
increment does not complete P0 research/collaboration quality or P2 service/UI.

documents.text:
# Knowledge retrieval and source citations

Requires the preview's `runtime` feature. The complete offline pipeline is:

```sh
cargo run --locked --features runtime --example agent_research
```

It imports two Markdown files, chunks and indexes them, exposes a permitted
read-only search tool to a durable agent, writes a cited report, and verifies
both exact quotations against the archived tool evidence. The example model
is deterministic and free. Replace it with the existing gateway model adapter
for provider execution; tool permissions and citation checks remain the same.

## Extension contracts

`runtime::rag` separates four host-controlled interfaces:

| Interface | Built-in implementation | Replacement contract |
|---|---|---|
| `DocumentLoader` | `TextLoader`: bounded UTF-8 text/Markdown file | Return a validated document with stable ID, source, title and extracted text; host decides external access |
| `Chunker` | `WindowChunker`: character windows with overlap | Preserve exact source text, UTF-8 byte offsets and provenance through `Chunk::from_range` |
| `CorpusStore` | `FileCorpusStore`: atomic versioned local snapshots | Consistent snapshots and atomic replacement/removal; enforce revision CAS when requested |
| `Retriever` | `LexicalRetriever`: deterministic BM25-style scores | Rank IDs in the exact supplied snapshot; obey top_k; finite nonnegative scores, no duplicate/unknown IDs |

The default lexical path requires no embeddings or external service and supports
basic Unicode words and individual CJK characters. Optional snapshot-bound vector
indexes and reciprocal-rank hybrid retrieval are described in
[research tools](research-tools.md). Embedding/index service credentials and
charges remain separate from generation budgets. Language-specific segmentation
and reranking remain extension work; no benchmark parity is claimed.

`Document` contains host-assigned `id`, `title`, display `source`, UTF-8 `text`
and bounded metadata. The plain loader accepts at most 8 MiB, rejects invalid
UTF-8, and does not execute Markdown/HTML or fetch URLs. The optional `research`
feature adds bounded HTML/web and trusted Poppler PDF extraction. Office formats
still require a host loader. Sources are data; their references are not
automatically followed. This library does not sandbox custom loaders.

`ingest` validates document and plugin chunks before changing storage. Importing
the same document ID atomically replaces its prior chunks; it does not append
stale versions. A chunk ID hashes its document ID, title, source, exact text and
byte range. Updated provenance/content produces a new identity. Remove uses the
same optional expected-revision contract; stale CAS operations fail without
mutating the existing corpus.

File storage captures an absolute root, serializes writers with an OS lock,
validates existing snapshots, and atomically replaces `corpus.json`. The default
snapshot limit is 64 MiB, 10,000 documents and 100,000 chunks. It is intended for
small local collections. Large collections should replace the store/retriever
with indexed database snapshots. Corrupt or unsupported corpus versions fail
closed. Corpus format is `CORPUS_VERSION = 1`.

## Tool integration and bounded search

```rust,no_run
use std::sync::Arc;
use taskloom::runtime::{ToolRegistry, ToolPolicy};
use taskloom::runtime::rag::*;

let corpus = Arc::new(FileCorpusStore::new("state/knowledge"));
let mut tools = ToolRegistry::new();
tools.register(RagTool::new("knowledge_search", corpus, Arc::new(LexicalRetriever)))?;
let policy = ToolPolicy::default()
    .allow("knowledge_search")
    .grant("knowledge:read");
# Ok::<(), taskloom::runtime::RuntimeError>(())
```

The tool takes `{ "query": "...", "top_k": 5 }`. Query bytes, hit count and
the complete serialized result have explicit limits. The default tool output
limit is 24 KiB. Search drops whole chunks that do not fit rather than modifying
the original text or inventing offsets. The result counts them in
`skipped_oversize`, so a caller (and the model) knows higher-ranked evidence
was left out. An empty hit list is valid; it is not
evidence for an answer. Every result includes corpus revision, exact chunk
text, title, source and original byte range. A denied tool is not exposed or
executed. Its read-only effect permits ordinary durable recovery; importing or
deleting documents is a separate explicit host action.

Retrieved text can contain malicious instructions. The supplied examples treat
it as untrusted evidence in the system prompt, and tool policy independently
controls capabilities. Prompt wording does not provide a security sandbox.
External retriever service charges are outside the agent's model-spend budget.

## Citation verification and its limits

Ask the model for `CitedReport { text, citations: [{ chunk_id, quote }] }`.
The text uses `[[full_chunk_id]]` references. Validate it using the actual
`SearchResult::verify` from the run's tool output, not a new search of a possibly
updated corpus. Verification rejects unknown/unretrieved sources, duplicate
citations, chunks whose text no longer matches their own ID, absent or invented
quotes, quotes below the minimum size, absent/unclosed markers and references
without corresponding citations.

A quote must be an exact substring of the cited chunk and long enough to be
meaningful: by default at least 12 non-whitespace characters, or 3 words, or
6 CJK (Han/kana/Hangul) characters, whichever is met first. Use
`SearchResult::verify_with`/`verify_all_with` and `QuotePolicy` to change
these minimums; `verify`/`verify_all`, the app and benchmarks use the default.

What this proves, precisely: each cited chunk appeared in the supplied tool
output, its ID equals the hash of its own content, and the quote occurs in it.
The chunk ID is a *self*-hash. It detects accidental corruption, not tampering:
whoever can edit archived tool output can edit a chunk and recompute its ID,
and the edited chunk then verifies. It is not compared with the original
document's hash or the current corpus, and the app accepts output of any tool
step named `knowledge_search`. Integrity therefore rests on the durable run
store. Binding evidence to a specific tool instance/corpus (for example signed
or store-anchored results) is future work.

`VerifiedReport` retains exact chunks and corpus revision, so a saved report
can still be audited after the corpus is updated or deleted. The durable run
also retains the full tool result. Store these artifacts for the required
retention period; the standalone example uses a temporary directory.

For multiple searches, use `SearchResult::verify_all` with their actual archived
outputs. Reports retain all `corpus_revisions`; `corpus_revision` is present only
when they agree. This avoids hiding updates between retrievals. The application
report endpoint gathers the run's recorded `knowledge_search` outputs this way.

Verification establishes provenance and exact quotation. It does not establish
that the source is correct, that a quotation supports a conclusion, or that all
prose is supported. Evaluate those separately, optionally with the bounded
reviewer workflow. Source/display paths may reveal local details; access
control, source redaction and private-corpus retention are host concerns.
