# Research sources and hybrid retrieval

`research` adds bounded webpage/search clients and an explicitly configured
Poppler PDF loader. `app` includes this feature but grants no web or PDF access
by default. Vector/hybrid retrieval is available with `runtime` alone.
These additions do not change the existing `AgentTask` API.

## Web sources and search

Merge the relevant section into the application's configuration:

```json
{
  "research": {
    "web": {
      "allowed_origins": ["https://www.rust-lang.org", "https://rust-lang.org"],
      "allow_private": false,
      "max_body_bytes": 2097152,
      "max_text_bytes": 131072,
      "max_redirects": 2,
      "timeout_ms": 15000
    },
    "search": {
      "endpoint": "https://api.search.brave.com/res/v1/web/search",
      "key_env": "BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY",
      "namespace": "my-search-tenant-v1",
      "access": {
        "allowed_origins": ["https://api.search.brave.com"],
        "allow_private": false,
        "max_body_bytes": 262144,
        "max_text_bytes": 131072,
        "max_redirects": 0,
        "timeout_ms": 15000
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Omit `search` when no search account/key is available. Key values are read from
the named environment variable; never commit them. Search supports the Brave
Web Search JSON contract (`web.results`), not an arbitrary search response
format. It returns titles, URLs and snippets as unverified leads. Returned URLs
never expand the web fetch allowlist. Search-service charges are separate from
the generation `RunBudget`; configure service quotas and inspect its billing.

```sh
taskloom --config research.json web-search "Rust async cancellation"
taskloom --config research.json import-web rust-learn "Rust learning" https://www.rust-lang.org/learn
taskloom --config research.json search "Rust"
```

`WebClient` grants exact HTTP(S) origins, including ports. Wildcards, embedded
credentials and fragments are rejected. Every redirect must remain within
granted origins; HTTPS downgrade is denied. DNS results are checked against
private/reserved address ranges and pinned per connection to resist rebinding.
System proxies, cookies and automatic redirects are disabled. Private network
access requires the separate explicit `allow_private: true` opt-in; use it
only for deliberately configured internal sources or local fixtures. Search
credentials are never forwarded through redirects.

Responses have total deadlines, hop limits and streamed byte limits, even
without Content-Length. Only UTF-8 HTML/plain text/Markdown is accepted.
HTML extraction excludes scripts, styles, templates, SVGs and frames; it never
executes JavaScript or fetches subresources. `timeout_ms` covers the whole
fetch including extraction. At most four HTML workers run concurrently.
The HTML5 tokenizer handles quoted attributes, raw text and foreign content;
a guarded tree builder checks the deadline per token and bounds its live
open-element/formatting references to 512. Input is fed in bounded UTF-8 chunks
with deadline checks, so tokenization also stops without requiring a closing
tag. An expired request cannot leave an unrestricted full-document parse
running. Text extraction then traverses the tree once, skipping excluded
subtrees. Script-rendered pages, login flows,
OCR, bot challenges and other encodings are unsupported and require a suitable
host-controlled loader. Sources remain untrusted data.

Imported documents retain requested/final URL, response-body SHA-256, extraction
version and network configuration identity. Chunk offsets refer to extracted
UTF-8 text. Search snippets alone do not establish source support. Import the
original page into the corpus, retrieve its chunks and verify exact quotations.

## PDF import

Install Poppler from a trusted OS/package source and configure its explicit
executable path; no binary is downloaded or guessed automatically:

```json
{
  "research": {
    "pdf": {
      "executable": "/usr/bin/pdftotext",
      "extractor_id": "poppler-pdftotext-your-installed-version",
      "max_input_bytes": 8388608,
      "max_text_bytes": 8388608,
      "max_pages": 500,
      "timeout_ms": 15000
    }
  }
}
```

On Windows select the installed `pdftotext.exe`; JSON backslashes must be
escaped. Relative executable paths resolve against the config file directory.
Keep `extractor_id` aligned with the installed/pinned binary version. The loader
runs this trusted parser as the host user, without a shell. This parser is not
a hostile-code sandbox; use an isolated host/parser service for adversarial PDFs.

```sh
taskloom --config research.json import-pdf report "Research report" ./report.pdf
```

The loader takes a bounded private copy, validates the PDF header and records
its original SHA-256. Extraction enforces input/output/page/time limits and kills
the child on failure. Empty/scanned, encrypted or malformed PDFs fail explicitly;
there is no automatic OCR or network fallback. Form-feed characters delimit
pages. Citations refer to extracted UTF-8 byte ranges, not offsets in the binary
PDF, and do not imply visual-layout or OCR accuracy.

## Application API and UI

All routes require the existing bearer token:

| Method/path | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/research/capabilities` | Enabled source types, granted fetch origins and retrieval binding; no keys |
| `POST /api/research/search` | `{query,count}` with count 1–10; unverified search leads |
| `POST /api/knowledge/web` | `{id,title,url,expected_revision}`; fetch/extract then atomic corpus import |
| `POST /api/knowledge/pdf` | `{id,title,filename,data_base64,expected_revision}`; upload bytes only, never a host file path |

The console supports PDF upload, web search and explicit webpage import. The
existing 1 MiB HTTP body and 750 KB UI upload limits apply; larger PDFs use the
CLI. Models receive `web_search` and `web_fetch` only when configured. Roles must
also explicitly allow those names. Both tools are read-only network capabilities;
they do not silently modify the corpus or grant further access. Tool definitions
freeze nonsecret endpoint/tenant/network policy identities for durable reentry.

## Vector indexes and hybrid search

`EmbeddingModel` is the host-owned embedding interface. `ProviderEmbeddingModel`
adapts an existing `Provider` (including OpenAI-compatible embeddings), with an
explicit model, tenant namespace, input-byte ceiling and per-call deadline.
It does not retry or change models. The configured identity is not proof of the
actual model served by a proxy. Provider responses must remain in input order.
Embedding-service usage/charges are separate from the generation budget and
are not included in task benchmark model-cost totals.

`EmbeddingIndex::build` explicitly embeds the supplied corpus in batches of at
most 32. It stores model identity and a full corpus fingerprint, with 1–4096
dimensions, at most 10,000 chunks and 4 million total vector values. Indexes are
serializable; hosts should persist them atomically and load with a size limit.
No automatic paid rebuild occurs. Replaced/deleted documents, metadata changes
or a different corpus revision require an explicit rebuild. Invalid dimensions,
zero/nonfinite vectors, changed identities and stale snapshots fail before a
query service call.

```rust,no_run
use std::sync::Arc;
use taskloom::runtime::rag::*;
# async fn example(snapshot: CorpusSnapshot, model: Arc<dyn EmbeddingModel>) -> Result<(), taskloom::runtime::RuntimeError> {
let index = EmbeddingIndex::build(&snapshot, model.as_ref()).await?;
let vector = VectorRetriever::new(index, model, &snapshot)?;
let hybrid = HybridRetriever::new(Arc::new(LexicalRetriever), Arc::new(vector));
let results = hybrid.retrieve(&snapshot, &RetrievalQuery::new("research question")).await?;
# let _ = results;
# Ok(()) }
```

`VectorRetriever` uses positive cosine similarity by default. A host-calibrated
`with_min_score` or application `retrieval.semantic_min_score` can filter weak
semantic candidates before fusion; no universal relevance cutoff is implied.
`HybridRetriever` combines
lexical and semantic rankings using weighted reciprocal rank fusion, with up
to 20 candidates per backend. Scores from different services are not directly
compared. Unknown/duplicate IDs and invalid scores fail before fusion; ties are
deterministic. A zero backend weight avoids its service call. A failed semantic
backend surfaces an error; it never silently substitutes lexical retrieval.

Use `Application::with_retriever` to share a host-built custom retriever between
the knowledge tool and operator search API. The standard CLI search and
`Application::open` now also support the host's `retrieval` configuration below.
The default remains local lexical search. Built-in vector/fusion identities are frozen into RAG tool
definitions. Custom backends should implement `Retriever::identity` and version
their own index/model/tenant contracts. Corpus updates while a hybrid host runs
fail closed until it is reopened with the matching rebuilt index.

## Default field retrieval and controlled aliases

The default lexical retriever scores body, title and selected metadata values
independently using BM25-style normalization and weights 1, 2 and 1. Default
metadata keys are `tags`, `keywords`, `topic`, `summary` and `author`. Ingestion
hashes, URLs and other technical metadata do not participate unless the host
explicitly includes their keys. Field matches only locate original chunks;
citations must still quote their **body**, not the title or metadata.

```json
{
  "retrieval": {
    "mode": "lexical",
    "lexical": {
      "body_weight": 1,
      "title_weight": 2,
      "metadata_weight": 1,
      "metadata_keys": ["tags", "keywords", "topic", "summary", "author"],
      "query_aliases": {"restart service": ["reconciliation", "interrupted writes"]}
    }
  }
}
```

Aliases match the entire trimmed, lowercased query and append configured terms
once. The original query is retained. No recursive rewrite, model call, source
instruction or permission change occurs. Configuration allows at most 64 rules,
8 aliases per rule, 512 bytes per alias/key and 4096 expanded query bytes.
Only the lexical leg is expanded; the semantic leg embeds the original query.
`POST /api/retrieval/explain` returns both queries without contacting a service.

## Explicit application embedding configuration

An embedding configuration can be present while mode remains `lexical`. This
allows the application to start and build its first index before enabling
hybrid queries. Nothing contacts the embedding service on startup, inspection,
configuration validation or lexical search.

This example uses a **zero-priced local service**, whose configured endpoint
must actually implement the OpenAI embedding protocol. It is not an included
model or an assumption that commercial services are free. Set the named dummy
key locally if your server requires no authentication; credentials are never
part of this file. Remote HTTP endpoints, URL credentials and query credentials
are rejected; remote services require HTTPS.

```json
{
  "retrieval": {
    "mode": "lexical",
    "embedding": {
      "provider": {
        "type": "openai",
        "base_url": "http://127.0.0.1:8081/v1",
        "key_env": "TASKLOOM_EMBEDDING_KEY",
        "namespace": "my-local-embedding-version-tenant"
      },
      "model": "your-installed-embedding-model",
      "currency": "USD",
      "input_micros_per_million_tokens": 0,
      "max_request_cost_micros": 0,
      "max_total_cost_micros": 0,
      "max_input_bytes": 131072,
      "timeout_ms": 30000
    },
    "lexical_weight": 1,
    "semantic_weight": 1,
    "semantic_min_score": 0,
    "rank_constant": 60,
    "candidate_k": 20
  }
}
```

For a paid service, configure its actual currency and input price, plus an
explicit per-request reservation and overall cap. One micro-unit is one
millionth of the currency unit: a price of USD 0.10 per million tokens is
`input_micros_per_million_tokens: 100000`. Choose a request reservation covering
the maximum accepted input under that service's documented billing contract.
This is local admission control, **not a provider-enforced invoice ceiling**.
If the service reports more than the reservation, the actual charge is saved
and further dispatch is blocked. Use provider account quotas for a hard external
billing limit. Local hardware/electricity costs are not metered here.

`state_dir/retrieval/spend.json` records embedding charges independently of the
generation `RunBudget`, web search and other tool-service charges. Each batch
or query reservation is flushed atomically under an OS lock **before dispatch**.
Known input-token usage settles the reservation with rounded-up micro-unit
pricing. Absent/invalid usage, cancellation, timeout or provider errors retain
the full reservation and remain unknown. There is no automatic retry, refund,
model fallback or background rebuild. Reported usage relies on the configured
service's truthfulness; a proxy identity does not attest to a particular model.
Other provider fees are not inferred from input-token prices.

The cap covers all processes sharing this state directory. Changing model,
endpoint, tenant, currency or price requires an explicit ledger migration;
binding mismatches fail rather than resetting spending. Do not delete a ledger
to recover an unknown charge. Reconcile it against the provider separately;
an operator reconciliation UI for this ledger is not yet implemented. Raising
the overall cap deliberately permits more requests. Index construction can
fail after paid batches; reservations and known charges remain recorded.

```sh
taskloom --config research.json index-status
# Copy the returned corpus_revision and configuration_binding exactly:
taskloom --config research.json index-build 3 CONFIGURATION_BINDING
```

`index-build` is also the explicit full **update** operation. It validates all
batch input sizes before the first request, holds an index-builder OS lock,
and saves a complete index atomically only after embedding succeeds and the
source snapshot still matches. It does not silently reuse partial failed work.
Saved indexes have a 128 MiB file limit and the existing vector/value limits.
Set `retrieval.mode` to `hybrid`, then restart the host to load the saved index.
The CLI loads the selected retriever for each invocation. In a running host,
operator search and model tools share one immutable retriever/index. Newly
built indexes require a host restart. Corpus changes invalidate the old index
before any paid query embedding; failed semantic retrieval does not fall back
silently to lexical search.

| Authenticated API | Operation |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/retrieval` | Configuration identity, corpus/index validity, active binding and separate embedding spending; no service call |
| `POST /api/retrieval/validate` | Validate an `AppRetrieval` JSON value without loading credentials, applying settings or contacting services |
| `POST /api/retrieval/index` | `{expected_revision,expected_binding}`; explicit full build/update using the current host configuration, may incur charges |
| `POST /api/retrieval/explain` | `RetrievalQuery`; inspect configured lexical expansion and original semantic query without searching |
| `POST /api/knowledge/search` | `RetrievalQuery`; search with the same active retriever as model tools, may incur embedding charges in hybrid mode |

The console can edit, validate and export the `retrieval` configuration property,
display index/spending status, explicitly build/update, explain a query and
search. Merge exported settings into the host configuration and restart to apply;
the export is a configuration **fragment**, not a replacement for other settings.
Index status is refreshed on request, not by an expensive background index scan.
The console never accepts key values or lets a retrieved document grant service
access. A full visual configuration wizard belongs to the unfinished P2 work.

### Migration

Old JSON configurations use the new lexical defaults automatically. Existing
`AgentTask` and unit-struct `LexicalRetriever` call sites remain valid. Rust
`AppConfig` struct literals listing every field must add `retrieval` or use
`..Default::default()`. Ranking changes are versioned as `lexical-v2` and frozen
into tool definitions; old suspended runs with the previous tool definition
must not be resumed under the new search contract. Finish them on their original
binary or start a new run. Administrative cancellation/rejection remains available.
Custom `Application::with_retriever` hosts keep their injected algorithm; the
explanation endpoint describes configured defaults and explicitly notes that a
custom backend may behave differently.

The OpenAI adapter now rejects wrong input counts, duplicate/gapped/out-of-range
embedding indices and malformed explicit indices before associating vectors with
source chunks. Responses omitting all indices retain their input-array order.

### Reproducible lexical relevance check

`tests/data/retrieval-quality-v1.json` contains 12 labelled operations documents,
16 positive queries, and two negative queries, with title/metadata-only cases,
Chinese queries and a misleading distractor. Run:

```sh
cargo test --locked --features runtime --test retrieval_quality -- --nocapture
cargo test --locked --all-features --test app_retrieval
```

The first prints per-query rankings, document recall@5, MRR@5 and negative-query
accuracy for the body-only and default-field configurations on the same corpus.
This small maintainer-authored regression set is visible to implementers; it is
not a held-out benchmark or evidence of general research quality. Quote matching
and claim support/factual accuracy remain distinct assessments. The second uses
real local HTTP, separate CLI processes and durable files with **protocol-fixture
vectors** to test index, authorization, reservation, timeout and restart behavior.
It does not establish real-model embedding relevance. The subsequent
[native local evaluation](native-evaluation.md) uses actual Qwen weights and
retains unsuccessful negative-query/agent outcomes. Broader quality and
cross-framework acceptance remain open P0 work.

For opt-in stop-word filtering, exact long alphanumeric query constraints,
configuration migration and actual learned-embedding calibration results, see
[retrieval relevance](retrieval-relevance.md). Empty/disabled settings preserve
old configuration bindings; source text and citable quotations are unchanged.

## Validation provenance

Local HTTP fixtures verify search→fetch→ingest→retrieve→quote verification,
credential isolation, redirects, private-address rejection, size/deadline/status
failures, API import and shared retrieval. Vocabulary embeddings are explicit
test fixtures: they verify vector/fusion behavior, not semantic recall quality.

On 2026-11-27 a real CLI fetch of `https://www.rust-lang.org/learn` followed the
permitted redirect to `https://rust-lang.org/learn/` and imported one document
as three chunks. An offline excerpt run completed and verified three archived
source quotations at zero generation cost. The browser separately imported the
same page and verified the saved report with no console errors. This proves
public-web ingestion and quote provenance on that source, not live-LLM research
quality, visual rendering fidelity or arbitrary-site compatibility.

On 2026-11-27 the real `/usr/bin/pdftotext` parser in Linux extracted a two-page
generated PDF and passed page/output-limit checks. Reproduce this separate
environment-dependent acceptance with:

```sh
TASKLOOM_TEST_PDFTOTEXT=/usr/bin/pdftotext cargo test --locked --features research --test agent_pdf -- --ignored
```

The default suite reports this test as ignored if not explicitly invoked.
Hosted search, real embedding recall and provider-generated research reports
require configured services and are not established by these fixtures.

# Explicit Linux-container Python execution

The optional `sandbox` feature exposes `CodeSandbox`, `DockerSandbox` and
`SandboxTool`. `app` includes the feature but registers no execution tool until
the host supplies `sandbox` configuration. Even then, only workflow roles that
list the tool receive it, unless `sandbox_top_level` is set. A missing Docker engine, missing
image or failed container never falls back to host Python or a host shell.

## Isolation contract

Only code is model-controlled. The host fixes the Docker CLI, local engine
socket/pipe, immutable audited image, platform, CPU/memory/output/time limits.
The model cannot select an executable, image, mount, network, package, device,
environment variable or Docker option. Code is sent through stdin, not shell
command text or host argv interpolation. The host passes only the code's byte
length and SHA-256 as supervisor arguments (`--code-bytes`, `--code-sha256`).
End of stdin alone does not prove the write completed, because an interrupted
controller also closes stdin. The supervisor therefore refuses to run anything
unless it received exactly the declared bytes with the declared digest. On
refusal it returns exit code 126 with a `sandbox supervisor refused code`
message, so an interrupted write never runs a prefix of approved code. If
`docker run` fails before it reads stdin, the returned error carries Docker's
exit status and stderr, not the resulting broken-pipe write error.
Before dispatch, a bounded engine capability query requires Linux, memory/swap/
PID/CPU limits, private cgroup namespaces and Docker's built-in seccomp profile.
Unsupported or unverified capabilities fail instead of relying on warnings
about ignored resource flags.

Each call runs a fresh Linux container with no network, no host bind mounts,
read-only root filesystem, a 16 MiB non-executable `/tmp`, 32-PID ceiling,
bounded CPU/memory/swap, file-descriptor/file-size/core limits, private IPC/
cgroup namespaces, Docker's normal seccomp policy and no-new-privileges.
There is no Docker socket, host credential, artifact export or package install
capability. Docker CLI configuration/environment is replaced with an empty
private config so host proxy variables/context credentials are not injected.

The supplied image's Python supervisor runs as **container PID 1 and uid 0**,
with only SETUID/SETGID capabilities. Its untrusted child runs as uid/gid 65534,
without those privileges, and cannot signal the root monitor. The monitor owns
the wall deadline and combined stdout/stderr byte ceiling. It returns a bounded
JSON packet and exits container PID 1 on timeout, excessive output or completion,
causing the container runtime to kill remaining namespace processes even if
they detached from the original process group. This deadline survives loss of
the host controller; it does not depend solely on killing `docker run`.
Ingress is also nonblocking and deadline-bound if the controller dies before
stdin EOF. Final response writing has a 500 ms grace before unconditional PID 1
exit, so an abandoned/nonreading output connection cannot keep code running.

`--rm` removes the container after completion. The host additionally requests
forced removal on normal return, timeout and dropped futures. Cleanup is bounded
and best-effort if the daemon/runtime is unavailable. Results expose
`container_name` and `cleanup_confirmed`; inspect an unconfirmed cleanup instead
of assuming resources were removed. A process/daemon crash can prevent host
cleanup; the audited container monitor remains the execution time boundary
while its Linux runtime is functioning. Resource limits are per call, not a
global Docker billing/concurrency account.

A container shares its Linux kernel with the worker host. This is not VM or
hardware isolation, a guarantee against kernel/runtime exploits, or support for
arbitrary hostile multitenant workloads. Use a dedicated VM/worker or implement
`CodeSandbox` against an appropriately isolated service for that threat model.
The Docker daemon/socket is a powerful host capability and must remain
operator-owned. The tool never exposes the socket to submitted code.

## Build and pin the trusted supervisor image

Use a running local **Linux** Docker engine. Resolve a trusted official Python
base image to an immutable digest, review `sandbox/python/supervisor.py`, build
the supplied Dockerfile, then pin the resulting image ID/digest. For Linux:

```sh
DOCKER=/usr/bin/docker
ENGINE=unix:///var/run/docker.sock
$DOCKER --host "$ENGINE" pull python:3.12-slim
BASE_IMAGE=$($DOCKER --host "$ENGINE" image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' python:3.12-slim)
$DOCKER --host "$ENGINE" build --platform linux/amd64 --build-arg BASE_IMAGE="$BASE_IMAGE" -t taskloom-sandbox:local sandbox/python
IMAGE=$($DOCKER --host "$ENGINE" image inspect --format '{{.Id}}' taskloom-sandbox:local)
```

The supervisor contract changed when the code-length/SHA-256 check was added:
`supervisor.py` now requires `--code-bytes` and `--code-sha256`. Rebuild
the image, which gives it a new digest, and update the pinned `image`. An
image built from an older supervisor rejects the new arguments, so every call
fails with a Docker execution error instead of running unchecked code. The 2026-11-27
acceptance record below names the earlier image and supervisor build-context
hash. It is historical evidence for that image, not for the current
supervisor.

Retain the resolved base and final image digests with your deployment evidence;
repeat production builds using those exact digests. The mutable tag above is
only an explicit base discovery step. Runtime execution accepts only
`sha256:64-lowercase-hex` or `repository@sha256:64-lowercase-hex`, and always uses
`--pull=never`. A digest must identify the **audited supplied supervisor image**;
an arbitrary image digest does not establish its safety. The entrypoint is
fixed to `/usr/local/bin/python3 -I -B /opt/taskloom/supervisor.py`.

On Windows select the installed `docker.exe` and the Linux engine's named pipe,
for example `npipe:////./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine`. TCP, SSH, Windows
containers and context/engine fallback are rejected. Choose `linux/arm64` only
with a matching audited image/worker; there is no platform auto-detection.

## Application configuration and approvals

Merge into your host config after replacing paths and the digest:

```json
{
  "sandbox": {
    "executable": "/usr/bin/docker",
    "endpoint": "unix:///var/run/docker.sock",
    "image": "sha256:REPLACE_WITH_64_LOWERCASE_HEX_IMAGE_ID",
    "platform": "linux/amd64",
    "memory_mib": 128,
    "cpu_millis": 500,
    "timeout_ms": 5000,
    "max_output_bytes": 16384
  }
}
```

The placeholder deliberately fails validation. Maximum bounds are 30 seconds,
64 KiB code, 64 KiB combined raw output, 1 GiB memory and two CPUs per call.
`cpu_millis: 500` means half a CPU. The container result reports exit code,
stdout/stderr, timeout/output-limit flags, image, named container, elapsed time
and cleanup confirmation. Non-UTF-8 output is displayed lossily after the raw
byte limit is enforced. Container/infrastructure charges are not generation
`RunBudget` amounts.

The registered tool is `python_sandbox`, permission `sandbox:python`, with a
single argument `{"code":"..."}`. A workflow executor role must explicitly
allow this name. Top-level runs (`POST /api/runs`, CLI `run`) and session
turns are not offered the tool unless the top-level config also sets
`"sandbox_top_level": true` next to `sandbox`. The default is `false`, and
setting it without a `sandbox` section is a configuration error. Tool
permissions are frozen per run, so toggling the flag affects reentry of
existing top-level runs like any other tool-policy change. The tool is conservatively NonIdempotent, so default durable
approval requires review of the exact code and worker binding before dispatch.
A decision never implicitly executes code: resume the run/parent separately.
Changed image/limits/engine contracts invalidate pending reentry. PEER planning,
writing and reviewing cannot acquire this effectful tool. Generic AgentTask
execution and default app configuration remain unchanged.

For a library host:

```rust,no_run
use std::sync::Arc;
use taskloom::runtime::{ToolRegistry, ToolPolicy};
use taskloom::runtime::sandbox::{DockerSandbox, DockerSandboxConfig, SandboxTool};
# fn example(config: DockerSandboxConfig) -> Result<(), taskloom::runtime::RuntimeError> {
let mut tools = ToolRegistry::new();
tools.register(SandboxTool(Arc::new(DockerSandbox::new(config)?)))?;
let policy = ToolPolicy::default().allow("python_sandbox").grant("sandbox:python");
// Pass tools/policy to the existing AgentLoop + DurableAgent controller.
# let _ = policy; Ok(()) }
```

## Acceptance and current limits

Default tests verify the security-relevant command contract, bounded config,
exact-code approval and frozen worker identity. These are configuration/control
tests, **not proof that an engine actually isolated a workload**.

The separate real-container suite observes uid/gid, denied root-monitor signals,
read-only filesystem, no socket/network/host secret, output capping, detached
child timeout and cleanup after an observed running controller is cancelled.
It also holds stdin open without code/EOF and requires the supervisor to exit.
It is ignored by default and requires the audited image and running engine:

```sh
export TASKLOOM_SANDBOX_DOCKER=/usr/bin/docker
export TASKLOOM_SANDBOX_ENDPOINT=unix:///var/run/docker.sock
export TASKLOOM_SANDBOX_IMAGE="$IMAGE"
cargo test --locked --features sandbox --test agent_sandbox -- --ignored --test-threads=1
```

A separate ignored test uses the real Docker CLI against an intentionally
absent local endpoint and requires failure before code dispatch. This test
passed on Windows on 2026-11-27. It proves the unavailable-engine failure path,
not container isolation. Run only that case without a built image using
`cargo test --features sandbox --test agent_sandbox actual_docker_cli_missing_engine -- --ignored`
after setting `TASKLOOM_SANDBOX_DOCKER`.

The hosted CI workflow includes explicit image-build/isolation acceptance and
retains resolved base/final image provenance. Its configuration is not evidence
of a successful run; GitHub account billing currently prevents hosted jobs.

2026-11-27: after the owner manually started Docker Desktop, all five separately
invoked environment tests passed on its Linux/amd64 engine. This includes actual
cgroup memory/swap/PID/CPU values and file limits, uid/gid, denied monitor signals,
read-only root, no network/host secret/socket, detached-child deadlines, output
limits, open stdin without EOF and cancellation cleanup. No labelled test
containers remained after the suite. The first deadline attempt exposed a
cross-UID `killpg` permission failure; the repaired monitor uses bounded response
writing and unconditional PID 1 exit without adding CAP_KILL.

Docker Hub download was unavailable. The build used the existing cached official
Python 3.11 slim-bookworm image at a fixed digest. The built image, supervisor
source hash and actual test evidence are recorded in
[sandbox acceptance](acceptance/sandbox-20261127.json). This proves these cases
on this local engine; hosted CI remains blocked by the GitHub account issue.
An earlier automatic rejection of starting Docker was resolved by the owner's
manual startup; no rejected startup command was retried through another route.

# Checkpoints, approval and recovery

Enable `runtime`. `DurableAgent` adds persistent execution to an `AgentLoop`
without changing the single-task API. `FileRunStore` is a local filesystem
backend; `RunStore`/`RunLease` are extension points for other stores.

```rust,no_run
use taskloom::runtime::{AgentLoop, DurableAgent, FileRunStore, Message};
# async fn example(agent: &AgentLoop<'_>) -> Result<(), taskloom::runtime::RuntimeError> {
let store = FileRunStore::new("run-state");
let durable = DurableAgent::new(agent, &store);
let state = durable.start("research-1", vec![Message::user("Research this topic")]).await?;
// In another invocation, reconstruct the same agent configuration:
let state = durable.resume("research-1").await?;
println!("{:?}", state.status);
# Ok(()) }
```

`create` only saves a runnable job. `start` saves and executes it. `resume`
continues paused/abandoned work; it returns an already finished, waiting for
approval or waiting for reconciliation state without dispatching more work.
`RunStatus` is authoritative for the current lifecycle; `RunReport` contains
the last stop reason, cumulative usage/counters and the conversation/events.

## Checkpoint contract

`RunState` contains a format version, monotonic revision, frozen configuration,
execution cursor, model/tool counters, budget snapshot, full conversation,
events, tool attempts, approvals and operator recovery records. Definitions,
schemas, permissions, model settings and limits must match on resume. Bump a
tool's advertised definition when its implementation contract changes; the
library cannot detect a code change behind identical metadata.
After such a bump, `resume`, approval and `RetrySafe` are rejected for older
runs, because they lead to dispatch under the frozen contract. Operations that
only terminate or record remain available: `cancel`, an approval rejection,
and the `RecordResult`/`Abort` reconciliations. Use them to finish paused,
approval-waiting or recovery runs (and their session turns) after an upgrade.
Format 2 also binds the exact initial-message boundary and persists context
projections. Development format-1 jobs require the earlier checkout; they are
not silently migrated or reset. See [sessions and context](sessions-and-context.md).
Provider credentials/endpoints, model profiles and prices belong to the host
application. Keep their intended contract and currency unit consistent when
reconstructing a run; they are not authenticated by `RunConfig`.

The file backend uses hashed run ids, a per-run OS lock, flushed temporary
files, atomic replacement and monotonic revision checks; saving a checkpoint
older than the stored revision fails with `Conflict` rather than reporting
success. The lock is held
throughout an invocation, including background file writes after an async
future is dropped. Other workers receive `Conflict`; they cannot execute the
same run concurrently. Persistent lock files are never unlinked. `inspect`
does an atomic read of the last committed checkpoint without acquiring the
execution lock, so status can be viewed while a worker is active.
The final lease owner explicitly unlocks the file, including when another
process briefly inherited a duplicate descriptor; active background writes
keep ownership until they finish.

Checkpoints are saved before model calls, before tool dispatch and after each
result. If persistence fails, no subsequent operation is dispatched. A result
that exists only in memory is not treated as durably complete. Malformed,
inconsistent or future-version checkpoints are rejected rather than reset.
The default maximum file size is 64 MiB, configurable on `FileRunStore`.
Before dispatch, a run reserves its declared maximum reply size plus duplicate
tool state, context and terminal metadata. It stops with `StorageLimit` if that
allowance cannot fit. The allowance always includes room for an operator's
terminal record (about 21 KiB: actor and note stored twice, escaped), so a run
that was admitted can still be cancelled, aborted or reconciled under the cap. Native model replies are capped by
`RunLimits::max_model_result_bytes` (64 KiB by default); tool outputs use
`max_tool_result_bytes`. A reply that violates its declared byte ceiling is
not retained: the saved run is terminal, observed charges remain, and resume
cannot replay the call. See [session storage admission](sessions-and-context.md#session-size-limit)
for parent commit reservations and small-store configuration.

This provides process-crash recovery on a local filesystem, not a distributed
lease or an atomic transaction with an external service. Power-loss durability
depends on filesystem/OS guarantees; Unix directory metadata is flushed after
replacement. Store directories contain sensitive conversation/tool data and
must be trusted and access controlled by the host application.

## Graceful pause and cancellation

`DurableAgent::with_pause(&CancelToken)` requests a pause at the next completed
operation/checkpoint, before the following dispatch. It lets the active model
or tool finish. Resume using a fresh controller/pause token.

The agent's explicit or ambient cancellation token still interrupts active
work. Cancellation and exhausted limits are terminal; `resume` does not
silently reactivate them. In-flight tools remain marked uncertain for audit.
Recording a known result afterward does not reactivate a cancelled run.
`DurableAgent::cancel` records the operator's actor and note for an unowned
run. To attribute a cancellation of a live worker the same way, give it a
`CancelReason` with `with_cancel_reason`, call `record(actor, note)`, then
fire the cancellation token; the terminal checkpoint's detail reads
`cancelled by <actor>: <note>`. The application server does this for runs,
session turns and workflow children.

Step/tool limits and model spending accumulate across invocations. The elapsed
limit counts cumulative active execution, rounded up to milliseconds; known
pause/approval downtime is excluded. When a process dies during an operation,
the interval since its persisted wall-clock start is charged conservatively,
including unknown downtime. A backwards wall clock at recovery is rejected.

## Approval of exact input

Persistent runs require approval for idempotent/non-idempotent effects by
default. `ApprovalPolicy` can additionally require reads/named tools, or let
the host explicitly preauthorize a different policy at creation. The tool
must still pass its ordinary allowlist, scope and schema checks.

`state.pending_approval()` exposes a request containing the run id, complete
tool call, frozen definition, attempt number and a SHA-256 ticket over those
values. `decide(run_id, ticket, ApprovalDecision)` saves an approval or rejection
with actor/note/time. It does not execute anything. An approved job becomes
paused and needs an explicit `resume`. A rejection is terminal. Another attempt
requires a new ticket; earlier approvals stay in the audit history.

The application must authenticate actors before accepting decisions. Ticket
hashes bind the decision to input; they are not authentication signatures and
do not protect against someone who can rewrite the entire trusted store.

## Interrupted tools and model attempts

A tool that was in flight when a worker stopped becomes `Uncertain`; the run
stops as `NeedsRecovery`. No tool is automatically retried, including reads.
Failed/timed-out/unusable results from a tool with effects also require
reconciliation. Use `reconcile` with a matching call id and an operator record:

- `RecordResult`: after inspecting the external system, supply the known
  result. It completes that exact call without invoking the tool again.
- `RetrySafe`: only read-only/idempotent tools are eligible. The same run/call
  ids are reused for tool-side deduplication. It requires fresh approval where
  the policy demands it and consumes another tool attempt. If the run
  finishes before the retry is dispatched (for example, the fresh approval
  is rejected, a limit is reached or the run is cancelled), the call stays
  pending and a session turn can still be closed: the earlier attempt was
  already reconciled, and the host result records that its outcome is unknown.
- `Abort`: terminate the run without continuing the uncertain operation. The
  call is resolved with an explicit error result recording the actor, note
  and an unknown external outcome, so the run can be closed and the abort
  cannot be repeated.

Non-idempotent operations cannot use `RetrySafe`. The library cannot determine
whether an email was sent, a remote write committed or spawned work is still
running. Verify the external effect before recording a result; dropping a
future cannot roll it back. Tool implementations must uphold their declared
effect/idempotency contract.

An abandoned model call can be retried as a new bounded model step. Its
reservation is persisted **before** dispatch in a separate versioned journal
bound to the run id. Recovery selects the newer journal/checkpoint generation
and charges unobserved in-flight reservations conservatively. A crash cannot
reset earlier cost or step counts. Missing reported usage remains unknown;
the ledger does not invent tokens for interrupted attempts.

Custom `Model` implementations must await `budget.reserve_before_dispatch`
for every paid attempt. Synchronous `reserve` is rejected with persistent
journaling. The built-in `GatewayTransport` follows this contract for retries
and fallback models. A journal failure prevents the provider request.

## Reproducible offline example

```text
cargo run --locked --features runtime --example agent_resume
```

The default demo creates a temporary workspace, waits for exact write approval,
reconstructs the controller, and creates a note once. It uses a deterministic
offline model. For separate process invocations, choose a new workspace:

```text
cargo run --locked --features runtime --example agent_resume -- start ./demo-state
cargo run --locked --features runtime --example agent_resume -- show ./demo-state
cargo run --locked --features runtime --example agent_resume -- approve ./demo-state
cargo run --locked --features runtime --example agent_resume -- resume ./demo-state
```

Review the printed request before running `approve`. The `save_note` tool uses
`create_new` and never overwrites a preexisting note. The example deliberately
does not auto-reconcile an interrupted non-idempotent write.

`tests/agent_durable.rs` also terminates actual child processes after an
external write/budget reservation, then verifies recovery, preserved costs,
fresh approvals, no duplicated effects, failed writes, exclusion and atomic
inspection. It uses no provider credentials.

# Durable workflows and PEER collaboration

Requires the `runtime` feature from the `v0.2.0-alpha.1` preview and Rust 1.86+. Run the complete
offline example with:

```sh
cargo run --locked --features runtime --example agent_peer
```

It runs four native durable model roles, plans two tasks, waits for explicit
approval of two real file writes, resumes, rejects the first draft and approves
the rewrite. It asserts two file effects, one planner call, two writer calls,
two reviewer calls, and no further dispatch on completed reentry. The model is
deterministic and local; this verifies orchestration, not model quality.

## DAGs and exact handoffs

`runtime::workflow` exposes `WorkflowDefinition`, `WorkflowNode`,
`WorkflowTasks`, `WorkflowRunner` and `FileWorkflowStore`. A node names a
registered `WorkflowTask`. Dependencies establish sequential ordering;
independent ready nodes run concurrently up to `max_parallel`. `Condition`
supports existence, equality, conjunction and negation over declared
dependencies. Missing handlers, cycles, undeclared condition/selector inputs
and duplicate identifiers fail before dispatch.

```rust,no_run
use taskloom::runtime::workflow::*;
use serde_json::json;

let graph = WorkflowDefinition::new([
    WorkflowNode::new("left", "research"),
    WorkflowNode::new("right", "research"),
    WorkflowNode::new("report", "writer")
        .after(["left", "right"])
        .select("evidence", "left", "/findings")
        .select("counterpoints", "right", "/findings"),
    WorkflowNode::new("publish", "publisher")
        .after(["report"])
        .when(Condition::Equals {
            node: "report".into(), pointer: "/approved".into(), value: json!(true),
        }),
]);
```

`NodeContext` contains the workflow/node IDs, a stable child run ID, original
workflow input, node parameters and dependency outputs. Selectors use JSON
Pointers. Without selectors, all declared dependencies are passed by name;
with selectors, only the selected aliases are passed. Skipped dependencies
skip successors unless `allow_skipped()` is explicit. A present JSON `null`
is a valid output and survives storage. Exact handoffs are checkpointed and
validated on load, rather than reconstructed from partial model text.

`AgentWorkflowTask` delegates to `DurableAgent::start_or_resume` with that
stable child ID. Its output can be text or locally schema-validated JSON.
Approval policy, role system prompt, model/run configuration and output
schema are frozen. Changed registration/configuration/limits reject resume.
Custom handlers must version their implementation contract explicitly;
configuration fingerprints cannot detect changed Rust code.

## Recovery and effects

The workflow saves an intent and spending allocation before polling a handler.
Completed nodes are never invoked again. Each handler declares one contract:

| Recovery | Implementer obligation | After process interruption |
|---|---|---|
| `Pure` | No effects, paid I/O or usage; zero cost ceiling | Safe recomputation |
| `DurableChild` | Reenter the exact stable child ID/input; child owns effects and spending journal | Reenter child and observe its state |
| `Manual` | Any other effectful implementation | Mark uncertain; operator must record observed output or abort |

These are host implementation contracts, not a sandbox. Effects must occur
inside the returned future. Cancellation and dropping a future do not undo
external operations. Tools keep their original read-only/idempotent/
non-idempotent metadata and exact-input approval rules.

Use `WorkflowStore::inspect` for atomic read-only status. It does not take
worker ownership or dispatch work. A file lease excludes concurrent workflow
controllers across processes. Failed checkpoint writes stop execution. If a
child completed but the parent's result checkpoint failed, reentry observes
the completed child without repeating its tools. Real process-death tests
also terminate after an external write and require child reconciliation.

For a native agent node waiting on approval, inspect `node.child.run_id`,
read its `RunState::pending_approval()`, then call the original role's
`DurableAgent::decide` with that ticket and actor/note. Resume the workflow
after decisions; merely approving does not dispatch tools. An uncertain tool
requires `DurableAgent::reconcile` on the child. Reentering the parent then
continues the existing child. A busy child remains waiting with unobserved
status; the workflow does not invent a successful outcome or release its
budget allocation.

Manual uncertain nodes use `WorkflowRunner::reconcile` with `RecordOutput`
(observed result/cost/usage) or `Abort`. `RetryPure` is restricted to pure
nodes in nonterminal workflows. Reconciliation records actor, note and time.
Every entry point that takes ownership (`resume` and `reconcile`) first
recovers a workflow whose previous controller died while `Running`: it charges
the downtime and turns the nodes that controller left running into `Pending`
(pure/durable) or `Uncertain` (manual), so reconciling one node never hides
another node's possible effect. A stored state with running nodes under any
status other than `Running` is rejected as corrupt.
Durable-child effects cannot be overridden through the parent's manual
reconciliation API. A native agent node whose child run has finished without a
usable final answer fails, naming the child run; a finished child cannot
change, so it is not re-dispatched.

## Limits, pause and cancellation

`WorkflowLimits` bounds nodes, parallelism, total dispatches (including child
resume probes), active duration, shutdown grace, output bytes and optional
model spending. Waiting for an operator between invocations does not consume
active duration. An abandoned running invocation conservatively charges wall
time until recovery; a backward wall clock fails closed. Passive inspection
does not spend dispatches. Repeated explicit resumes do, even if approval is
still pending, so poll status with `inspect`.

A global spending cap requires a per-task ceiling. The scheduler reserves
each admitted node's full ceiling, waits for concurrent settlements when
needed, and releases unused funds on completion. Native agent costs are
cumulative across child resumes and counted once. Unknown costs remain
charged at their ceiling and marked uncertain. Custom implementations must
enforce their declared paid-attempt ceilings; the runner cannot preempt an
arbitrary external client that ignores its contract. This cap covers model
spending, not independent external service/tool charges.

`with_pause` requests a graceful pause: finish admitted nodes, admit no new
ones, then checkpoint. `with_cancel` or a deadline signals child tokens and
drains up to `shutdown_grace`. Uncooperative manual tasks become uncertain;
durable tasks keep a child reference and allocation for direct inspection.
Cancellation, deadline, dispatch/budget exhaustion and failure are terminal;
`resume` does not reset their limits. Outstanding effects in a terminal
workflow must still be reconciled through their owning controller. A terminal
label is not proof that an external operation was undone.

Workflow state format is `WORKFLOW_STATE_VERSION = 1`. Run checkpoints retain
their separate format 2. Both reject unsupported versions and corrupt state.
File roots are captured absolutely at construction. Persisted messages,
outputs, exact inputs and events may contain private data; host access control
and retention remain the application's responsibility.

The event log is not capped: load-time validation checks every node's
dispatch counter against its `NodeStarted` events, so dropping old events
would weaken corruption detection. Its growth is bounded instead. A resume
that records nothing and ends in the status it started from (for example a
paused workflow resumed with the pause signal still set) leaves the log
unchanged and emits nothing to the event sink. Every other invocation either
dispatches (bounded by `max_dispatches`), changes status or resolves an
uncertain node, so the log grows with dispatches and node count, plus one
`Resumed` event per controller that died before recording anything else.

## Bounded planner/executor/writer/reviewer flow

Register four roles and call `PeerSpec::install(&mut tasks)` to construct a
bounded static graph. `PeerPlan::schema(max_tasks)` and `PeerReview::schema()`
provide JSON output contracts for model roles. The plan validator rejects
empty/oversized plans, duplicate task IDs and empty instructions.

1. Planner produces a bounded list of tasks.
2. Executors consume distinct task selectors concurrently, exactly once per
   completed child. Extra worker slots skip.
3. Writer consumes the plan and executor outputs.
4. Reviewer returns `{ "approved": bool, "feedback": string }`.
5. A rejected draft is rewritten with previous draft/feedback, within
   `max_revisions`; executor effects are retained. Approval skips later rounds.
6. `result` selects the first approved draft. Exhausted revisions fail rather
   than treating an unapproved draft as success.

Planner/writer/reviewer must be pure transforms or native durable agent roles
with only read-only tools. Put side effects in executors. This prevents a
review rewrite from implicitly repeating a publishing/write role. Tool
implementations still must tell the truth about effects. PEER provides basic
bounded coordination; distributed workers, arbitrary cyclic graphs, dynamic
team formation and semantic report quality evaluation are not implemented.

# Sessions and bounded model context

Enable `runtime`. Sessions retain full conversations across turns; context
projections bound the data sent to a model without rewriting that archive.
Use either capability independently or combine them with `DurableAgent`.

## Session lifecycle

`SessionManager` works with the `SessionStore` compare-and-swap contract.
`FileSessionStore` uses versioned JSON, hashed ids, per-document OS locks,
flushed atomic replacement and append-only history. Both file store types
resolve relative roots at construction, keeping their identity stable if a
host tool later changes process cwd. Store data in a trusted directory.

```rust,no_run
use taskloom::runtime::{AgentLoop, DurableAgent, FileRunStore, FileSessionStore, SessionManager};
# async fn example(agent: &AgentLoop<'_>) -> Result<(), taskloom::runtime::RuntimeError> {
let runs = FileRunStore::new("state/runs");
let sessions = FileSessionStore::new("state/sessions");
let manager = SessionManager::new(&sessions);
manager.create("chat", vec!["Follow the host's tool policy.".into()]).await?;
let durable = DurableAgent::new(agent, &runs);
let result = manager.run_turn(&durable, "chat", "turn-1", "Research this topic").await?;
// Reconstruct the same configured agent after restart:
let result = manager.resume_turn(&durable, "chat", "turn-1").await?;
println!("{:?}", result.run.status);
# Ok(()) }
```

Before any model request, `begin_turn` commits one active binding containing
the exact user input and a run id namespaced by session and turn id. Another
turn cannot enter that session while a job is running, paused or awaiting
approval/reconciliation. Distinct sessions can execute independently.

`run_turn` and `resume_turn` use `DurableAgent::start_or_resume`. They recover
both a crash before run creation and a completed run whose session commit was
interrupted. A duplicate turn id with the same input reuses its run; different
input is rejected. Committing the same final report twice does not append
duplicate messages. Concurrent metadata updates use revision CAS; `Conflict`
can be retried, but must never be treated as permission to start another job.

Only completed runs commit automatically. A failed terminal turn remains
bound until `abandon_turn` records an authenticated operator/application actor
and note. Uncertain/in-flight tools must first be reconciled through the
durable controller. Known observations stay in conversation history; calls
that were never dispatched receive explicit host error results. This includes
a call whose earlier attempt was reconciled with `RetrySafe` when the retry
itself never started; a call whose current attempt may have been dispatched
is never closed this way. An `Abort` reconciliation resolves the call with an
error result, after which the turn can be closed. A host note
records the failed outcome. This prevents an incomplete tool protocol from
leaking into the following model request, or a new question from silently
forgetting an uncertain write.

`commit_turn`/`abandon_turn` accept trusted controller state, not arbitrary
client-supplied JSON. The host application authenticates session access and
operator identity. A session is conversation state, not a cross-turn money
budget; each durable run keeps its own configured limits.

## Session size limit

Every turn's run starts from the full session history, and each checkpoint
rewrites the whole run state, so a long session eventually approaches the
store's byte limit (64 MiB by default for both `FileSessionStore` and
`FileRunStore`; keep the session limit at least as large as the run limit).
To avoid a run that completes but can no longer be saved or committed, work is
refused **before** it starts:

- `begin_turn` (and so `run_turn`) rejects a new turn with
  `RuntimeError::StorageLimit` once the serialized session exceeds half of the
  session store's limit. Nothing is bound or dispatched.
- The new input and the metadata needed to close its turn must also fit;
  oversized input is rejected before the active binding is written.
- Managed execution subtracts the complete session commit metadata from its
  byte allowance. A durable run reserves the largest declared model/tool
  response, duplicated tool state, context projection and a terminal-record
  margin before dispatch. Insufficient space produces `StorageLimit` without
  a model/tool call. Close that turn with `abandon_turn` as for any failed run.

`RunLimits::max_model_result_bytes` caps the serialized native `ModelOutput`
(turn plus serving model) at 64 KiB by default. Small custom stores should
configure a smaller ceiling, for example 512 bytes for bounded short answers;
`max_tool_result_bytes` also contributes to tool admission. Existing limit JSON
without the new field receives the default. A custom model that violates its
byte ceiling receives a persisted terminal `StorageLimit`: its reply is not
retained, observed cost stays charged, and reentry does not call it again.

Cancellation, approval rejection, `RecordResult`/`Abort` reconciliation and
`abandon_turn` do not run dispatch-admission checks. Actual writes still obey
store byte limits, but admission keeps room for them: every run admission
leaves about 21 KiB for a terminal record, and the session commit reservation
includes the longest `abandon_turn` acknowledgement (actor 256 bytes, note
4096 bytes, without control characters other than newline and tab). A run or
turn that was admitted can therefore always be cancelled or abandoned. Small
stores need that headroom: about 28 KiB for a run store and 40 KiB for a session
store that bounds runs. When the limit is reached, start a new session
(optionally seeding it with a summary from the old one); the existing session
and its history are kept unchanged. Custom `SessionStore`/`RunLease`
implementations opt in by returning their limit from `max_bytes`.

## Context projection

Opt in using `AgentLoop::with_context(ContextPolicy { .. })`. The default
single-task API and loops without a context policy keep their existing input
behavior. The byte ceiling includes taskloom's normalized serialized messages
and tool definitions, rather than a provider's entire HTTP body;
it is not a tokenizer. Gateway token/context-window checks still apply.

The projection keeps all leading system instructions, the current user
question and the latest complete block. An assistant tool request plus all
its results is an indivisible block, including batches with multiple calls.
Recent blocks are retained up to `keep_recent_blocks`; if necessary, fewer
older blocks are kept to fit the limit. Tool calls/results are never split.

Omitted history is compressed into a bounded, explicitly labeled **user-role
data** message. It is not elevated into a system instruction. The summary
takes the position of the newest omitted message: when older tool blocks of
the current turn are dropped, it follows the current question and precedes
the retained recent blocks, so the chronology stays intact. The built-in
`ExtractiveCompressor` preserves bounded excerpts of recent omitted entries,
including tool ids/results. It is lossy: it does not guarantee retention of
every fact or infer a semantic summary. Keep critical task state in explicit
application data or retrieve it from the full session archive.

Implement `ContextCompressor` for domain-specific/precomputed summaries, and
select it with `with_context_compressor`. It must be deterministic, return
promptly and perform no paid I/O or effects. Version its stable id whenever
its contract changes. Model-generated summaries should be computed/accounted
as explicit application work, not hidden inside this synchronous hook.

The full transcript stays in `RunReport.messages`. `ContextRecord` saves the
source fingerprint, retained indices, exact summary, byte sizes and step id.
It reconstructs the actual input for inspection and is persisted before a
model dispatch. Recovery of an interrupted model reuses the saved projection
without calling the compressor again. Altered sources, split tool blocks,
changed compressor identity or over-budget projections are rejected.

If protected instructions/question, schemas and the latest tool block cannot
fit even with older material compressed, the run stops with `ContextLimit`
before a model request. It does not silently truncate a tool observation.

## Format and examples

Run checkpoints now use **format 2**, adding the exact initial-input boundary
and context projections. Development format-1 checkpoints are not silently
upgraded or reset: finish them with the prior checkout, or start a new run.
Single-task answer recording/cache formats and `AgentTask` are unchanged.
Sessions have their own format version 1.

```text
cargo run --locked --features runtime --example agent_session
```

The deterministic offline demo opens two turns, reconstructs the session store,
uses a compressed preference excerpt, preserves the original messages, then
repeats a turn without another model request. It makes no paid calls.

Tests in `agent_session.rs` cover restart windows, approval occupancy, exact
input binding, stale/concurrent revisions, failed-turn cleanup and uncertain
effects. `agent_context.rs` covers native tool correlations, Unicode/JSON byte
limits, frozen projections and compressor-free recovery after interruption.

documents.text:
# SQL identities and a project-scoped JSON service

With both `app` and `database`, the optional `app::multiuser::router` mounts
host-registered project Applications at `/tenants/T/projects/P/api/...`.
SQL stores users, project roles, token hashes, expiration, revocation and an
append-only administration audit. Every request authenticates the actual bearer
and freshly checks its SQL project membership. Request ownership fields cannot
choose an Application, state root, credential or tool grant.

This is a bounded identity/service increment. Project Applications use file
journals by default or explicitly configured [SQL persistence](sql-application.md).
SQL-backed Applications also enforce explicitly configured
[project generation quotas](generation-quota.md) across all run writers. The
explicit [durable queue and independent workers](durable-queue.md) add
cross-process admission/control/recovery and bounded local load evidence.
The existing single-operator `router`/CLI/UI remains available; selecting
it does not enable the new multi-user boundary.

Queue submission and resume require runner authority; queue control requires
operator authority, with actor identity supplied by authentication. Approvers
retain exact-ticket routes, and reconciliation still requires operator authority.
Once a project has a queue policy, direct execution/control endpoints are refused
in this service, including while queue admission is disabled. See the queue
document for immutable inputs, cross-process state and explicit continuation.

## Roles and identity

| Role | Allowed operations |
| --- | --- |
| reader | Inspect shared project runs/workflows/sessions/knowledge/configuration; pure configuration and workflow previews |
| runner | Reader operations plus task/session/workflow submission, explicit resume and configured retrieval queries |
| approver | Reader operations plus exact run/session/workflow-child approval or rejection |
| operator | All preceding operations, pause/cancel/abandon, explicit uncertain-effect reconciliation, knowledge management/index builds and explicit telemetry export |

Each account has one role per tenant/project and can belong to up to 64 projects.
Roles are not a hierarchy: approvers cannot submit/resume and runners cannot
approve. Project tool/skill/credential authority remains the trusted host's
configuration. A runner can select the host's registered roles; there is no
additional per-role ACL in this increment. Exact approval remains a separate
required operation for configured effects. Approval never dispatches a tool.

Project members with read authority share its run, workflow and session history;
these are not private per-user conversations. User-private memory endpoints and
memory-aware session turns are unavailable here. The router refuses a project's
fixed single-operator `AppMemory` configuration rather than giving every member
that owner's memory. The new SQL memory persistence primitive is independent;
authenticated per-user memory API integration remains unfinished. A host must
explicitly select state intended to be shared when mounting existing journals.

`SqlIdentityStore` is a trusted administration primitive, not an unrestricted
HTTP configuration API. `put_user` requires the expected catalog revision.
`issue_token` creates a bearer with two independent random UUID-v4 values
(244 random bits), persists only SHA-256 and returns its plaintext once in a
type with neither Debug nor Serialize. Lifetimes are 1 second–366 days. The
example issues 24-hour tokens to a new private file and prints only receipt
metadata. It never overwrites an existing file or prints the bearer/database URL.
Unix files use mode 0600; Windows files inherit the destination's ACL.

`AuthenticatedActor` has no public constructor/Deserialize. `authorize` rereads
SQL even for an already-created actor; revocation, membership removal and role
changes affect the next authorization without server restart. Disabling a user
also permanently revokes its existing tokens; reenabling requires new issuance.
Expiry uses database time. Revocation does not retroactively cancel an already
authorized active operation. Cancellation remains explicit.

For approval, cancellation, abandonment and reconciliation routes, the middleware
sets `actor` from authenticated identity before the existing typed handler sees
the body. A client-supplied actor cannot impersonate an operator. The saved exact
tool input, ticket and host tool contract remain unchanged. Body size remains
bounded to 1 MiB. Future application routes inherit no permission: the service
uses an explicit method/path allowlist and refuses ambiguous encoded paths.
An inaccessible known operation returns 403, missing/expired/revoked credentials
401, and an unavailable identity database 503; unknown routes can return 404.

Project state roots must be absolute and canonically disjoint. Store-directory
aliases/junctions that escape the project root are refused at startup. These
checks assume a trusted filesystem administrator; changing symlinks behind the
running service is not a supported tenancy mechanism. The root single-operator
API, static UI and identity-administration endpoints are not mounted by this
router. It is a JSON service; the existing UI remains single-operator.

## Reproducible local example

From the repository root:

```powershell
cargo build --locked --features app,database --example multiuser_host
$env:TASKLOOM_DATABASE_URL='sqlite://target/service-identities.sqlite?mode=rwc'
target/debug/examples/multiuser_host.exe migrate
target/debug/examples/multiuser_host.exe put-user examples/service/alice.json 0 bootstrap
target/debug/examples/multiuser_host.exe issue alice target/alice.private-token bootstrap
target/debug/examples/multiuser_host.exe serve examples/service/host.json
```

Use `catalog` only as the trusted local administrator to inspect the current
revision before later `put-user` calls. The example JSON selects an explicitly
offline model and no tools, with an explicit zero model cap. It is not native
model evidence. A separately reviewed project config can select a native model,
its credential environment, known prices and spending limit using the ordinary
Application configuration; the identity layer does not grant a paid endpoint.

In another terminal, read the issued token locally into an Authorization header
and call `GET http://127.0.0.1:18083/tenants/team-a/projects/main/api/identity`,
then `POST .../api/runs` with `{"id":"example","prompt":"Acknowledge this task."}`.
Alice has no team-b membership. Do not put bearer values in shell history,
source files, URLs or model prompts. Revoke by the printed nonsecret token ID:

```powershell
target/debug/examples/multiuser_host.exe revoke TOKEN_ID bootstrap
```

The tested transport is loopback HTTP. Exposing bearer authentication to remote
clients requires a separately configured TLS endpoint/reverse proxy. No hosted
identity provider, browser sign-in, secret delivery channel or TLS certificate
provisioning is claimed. Database credentials remain host-managed; an SDK/database
administrator can change grants and must be trusted.

## Migration, bounds and recovery

Run `migrate` explicitly before admitting requests. Identity records add the
`identity` family in the existing schema-v1 record table, with a reserved host
control namespace and envelope/revision validation. No existing file state or
single-operator bearer is silently imported; create accounts and explicit
memberships first. No automatic schema downgrade or bulk legacy migration exists.

The transactional catalog is bounded to 1,024 users, 4,096 issued token records
and 20,000 administration events, plus the database record byte limit. Admission
fails atomically when full. Automatic token/audit compaction is not implemented;
do not treat this bounded catalog as an unbounded identity provider. Failed CAS
updates leave the original catalog unchanged. A database outage fails closed.
Keep SQL credentials, the database and issued bearer files outside source.

The SQL Application backup example in `sql-application.md` verifies core state,
skills, indexes/ledger and identity metadata for SQL projects. File-backed
projects still need a coordinated backup of their file trees. Full deployment
and credential-rotation acceptance remains a P2 gate. Restoring
older identity data can also restore older revocation state; admission must
remain stopped until operators review/rotate credentials. Historical audit has
no bearer plaintext. No whole-application backup claim is made here.

## Acceptance

```powershell
cargo test --locked --features app,database --test database_identity --test app_multiuser sqlite
# Privately set TASKLOOM_TEST_POSTGRES_URL to the owned PostgreSQL fixture.
cargo test --locked --features app,database --test database_identity --test app_multiuser postgres -- --ignored
python examples/service/accept.py target/my-service-check --example target/debug/examples/multiuser_host.exe --postgres-fixture target/my-owned-postgres
```

Both real databases passed role/expiry/revocation/CAS and actual loopback HTTP
checks. Fixture-model requests produced actual fsynced file effects only after
exact approval; spoofed decision actors were replaced, foreign tenants refused,
and a panic after a real append retained an in-flight operation. Explicit reentry
marked uncertainty without another model/tool call; only an operator could
reconcile the observed result. Session and workflow-child approval/control paths
are verified separately with no extra external write.

A separate actual service executable/admin-process campaign passed ten controls
per database: scopes/roles, completed file journals, live downgrade/revocation,
no plaintext in SQL and cold restart with unchanged state. Its model is explicitly
offline. These are real storage/transport/authority checks, not native generation
quality, load/throughput, overall P2 completion or framework leadership evidence.
Initial test expectation mistakes and an invalid partial-limits example startup
are retained in `acceptance/p2-multiuser-20261128.json` with the repaired reruns.
